## 2026-10-05 (pass KV): grade 1 Sky, water and living things at the full standard, and the grade 1 science earmark

- Mikey, after KU: "Continue, not committed", so KT, KU and KV share the commit message. This is the third grade 1 course in the review ledger's order, three modules, lesson, story and bank together (Fable 5.1).
- 19 TAC 112.3 (Science, Grade 1, Adopted 2021, effective April 26, 2022) was read in full on Cornell LII, and the NGSS performance expectations 1-ESS1-1, 1-ESS1-2, 1-LS1-1, K-LS1-1 and 2-PS1-4 were read in their published words. The plan was labeled 2021 and cited three codes that are not in that section: "1.8C, identify characteristics of the Sun and the Moon and describe their patterns" exists in no published text; "1.5B" and "1.9A" are the 2010 numbering, which the 2021 standard replaced. The same disease the grade 2 Magnets citation has (accuracy item A3) was in grade 1 too. The 2021 grade 1 standard has no Sun and Moon expectation at all; Texas teaches them in grade 2 (2.9A), and the grade 1 Earth and space expectation is the seasons (1.9), which no lesson teaches. So Patterns in the sky is cited to 1.5A (identify and use patterns to describe phenomena) and to NGSS 1-ESS1-1 and 1-ESS1-2, Water changes to 1.6B, 1.8A and 1.8B, and What animals need to 1.12A and 1.13A, every row quoted from the published text.
- The three lessons were four spoken lines each with no prose, and their banks could make six, five and five different questions for a round of five, the bare minimum. Each now has prose, a key idea, an example and a nine-line script. Patterns in the sky: the sun comes up in the east and goes down in the west every day, low in the morning and high at midday, and it only looks as if the sun moves because the Earth turns; a pattern is something that happens the same way again and again, so you can say what will happen tomorrow; the moon shines with sunlight and seems to change from a thin curve to half to full and back in about a month, and is sometimes up by day; stars come out at night in the same patterns and the bright sun hides them by day; long summer days and short winter days; never look straight at the sun. Water changes: ice is frozen water, heat melts it and cold freezes it again; boiling makes steam and steam cools back into drops; a puddle dries into the air; if you know what heat and cold do you can predict (an ice pop in the sun, a cup of water in the freezer); melted butter and candle wax harden again, and a cooked egg or a baked cake never goes back; a stove cooks, a dryer blows hot air, and hot things burn. What animals need: food, water, air and a safe place to live; living things grow and make young, and a toy does not; a fish uses its fins and gills and has scales, a bird its wings, feathers and beak, a dog its legs, fur, teeth and nose; where each lives; and people copy animal parts, a helmet from a shell, a coat from fur, swim fins from fins.
- The banks grew to twenty, eighteen and twenty-two different questions (sixteen new kinds), every explanation with its reason, and a star joined the question icons for the night-sky question. Every young-learner question names the picture it shows, and the two-answer sort of question stays at the pace of the course.

The expectations the lessons teach are (5)(B) (steady beat in excerpts from various periods and cultures), (6)(C) (same/different between beat/rhythm, higher/lower, louder/softer, faster/slower) and (1)(C) (the words allegro and largo for tempo and forte and piano for dynamics), which no lesson had taught, and the NCAS text MU:Re7.2.1a, which the plan had cut ("(such as beat or pitch)" and "for a purpose"), is quoted in full with MU:Re8.1.1a beside it.

Each lesson now has an eight-line script, prose, a key idea and an example drawn by the app. The steady beat teaches the beat as the even pulse under a song, kept with hands and feet; the rhythm as the pattern of long and short sounds on top, so beat and rhythm are told apart; tempo as the speed of the beat, with allegro for fast and largo for slow; and a beat in music from every time and place. High and low teaches pitch, bigger things usually lower, a child's voice higher than a grown-up's, the piano climbing to the right, a tune going up and down, and the voice sliding from a growl to a squeak. Loud and soft teaches dynamics with their jobs (a lullaby for one sleepy listener, a parade drum for a street), forte and piano and why the piano is called that (pianoforte, the first keyboard that could play both), and growing louder and fading as changes in dynamics and not in pitch or tempo. The banks grew to fourteen, eleven and eleven different questions with four new kinds, every choice a capitalized whole, and every explanation with its reason. The three stories already matched their lessons and stayed. No new paintings.

Flat shapes (1.6A, 1.6B, 1.6D) teaches sides and vertices as the words that name a shape, the rhombus and the hexagon beside the four kindergarten shapes, a square as a special rectangle and a special rhombus (both are true, and the lesson says why: four equal sides, and four square corners), what defines a shape and what does not (color, size, which way it turns), a tall thin triangle, a turned square and a stretched hexagon that keep their names, and sorting by the number of sides. Drawing shapes (1.6C) is a tracing module that draws all six, with rectangle, rhombus and hexagon strokes added to the pad, each said the way the strokes draw it. Solids and their faces (1.6E, 1.6B) teaches faces, edges and vertices, the rectangular prism with the cube as its special case the way a square is a special rectangle, the triangular prism with two triangle faces and three rectangle faces, the sphere, cylinder and cone with their flat faces counted, and the real things each is shaped like; a cone's point is never asked as a vertex, since books disagree on whether to count it. Joining shapes (1.6F) draws twelve composites, the same two triangles making a square, a bigger triangle, a rectangle or a rhombus depending on the join, squares making rectangles and a bigger square, three triangles a trapezoid (taught here, where the standard first needs it), six triangles or two trapezoids a hexagon, so the same target shape is made more than one way. Halves and fourths (1.6G, 1.6H, 1.G.A.3) teaches the whole, fair shares, halves and fourths with quarters as the other name, half of and fourth of, two halves and four fourths as the whole, the fourth smaller than the half of the same whole, halves cut three ways, and the non-examples, two or four pieces that are not the same size.

SolidPic draws the rectangular prism as a box longer than it is tall and the triangular prism as a tent. Two new picture kinds, shares (a circle, square or rectangle cut by name, with a shaded count) and joined (a composite drawn as its tinted pieces with the seams showing), and shares chips as tapped choices. Every drawing was rendered in the real built page and looked at; the cut shapes first drew with the dark theme's own colors and showed as black pieces, so they and the joined figures now use the paper palette like the other diagrams.

The rules test re-derives every kind from tables it does not share, and holds the inclusive rules: rectangle and rhombus are never offered as wrong names for a square, a square is never shown as a wrong picture when a rectangle or a rhombus is asked for, rectangular prism is never a wrong name for a cube, a cube is never a wrong picture for a rectangular prism, a piece set that can make the asked shape is never a wrong answer, and a yes-or-no about joining is checked against the table of what the pieces can make. Open number lines (1.2F, 1.2D, 1.NBT.B.3) teaches greater to the right and less to the left, an open line that shows only the numbers you need, counting the marks from a known number, a number between two numbers, which of two is farther right, ordering three numbers by tens then ones on the line, and counting on across a ten.

- The fourth exposure, as proposed to Mikey (not built; his call): a light review a few weeks after a lesson is mastered and its memory check passed, drawn from the same bank at the same difficulty, five questions, spoken for the early years. Timing by the forgetting curve: two to three weeks after the memory check, then, if passed, a second light review about six weeks later, and nothing more unless a later course needs the skill (where a memory check already reaches back across courses). Outcomes, three ways: a clear pass (four or five of five) ends the schedule for that lesson and the confidence score rises; a bare pass (three of five) keeps the schedule and brings the next review forward to one week with the misses re-asked first; a fail (two or fewer) sends the lesson back to practice at the full round, with its story offered again, and the lesson's prerequisites get one memory check each, since a fade that deep usually has a cause one step earlier. Nothing is shown to the child as a failure; the educator's report shows the lesson as "reviewing" with the date. Cost: no new content, one new round kind, one scheduler, educator settings to turn it off per student. If Mikey says yes, it becomes a pass of its own with its rules in ALGORITHMS.md and tests before any screen.

## 2026-10-07 (pass LU): First Steps (pre-K 4) part one at the refined standard: colors, same and different, the six matching lessons, more and fewer

- Mikey committed through LT. First Steps has eighteen modules, too many to review well in one pass, so it is split the way pass JR split it: part one here (Colors, Same and Different, the six matching lessons, More and Fewer), part two next (the sizes, Patterns, One, Two, Three, the three drawing lessons, Taking Turns and Helpers All Around), then the stories' tags and the course's long story.
- Angles. Each lesson gained two or three spoken lines that show its idea another way, each with a sentence in its prose. Colors: a stop sign, a blueberry, a lemon and a pickle beside the four anchors, sorting blocks by color, and naming the colors on your own clothes. Same and Different: a pair of socks, two red crayons from one box, and checking shape, color and size at cleanup time. Match the Vehicles: where each one goes (a car on the road, a train on a track, a boat on the water, a rocket into space), said aloud for the first time, and two cars outside. Match the Things: the butterfly's wings and the robot's arms and legs said aloud, and your own arms and legs. Match the Water Animals: how much bigger a whale really is than most fish, since the pictures draw them the same size, and the turtle, frog and duck named aloud. Match the Land Animals: the fox's pointy ears beside the cat's, the snail's one flat foot and the owl's big eyes, so every animal the matching questions show is now named in the lesson. Match the Shapes: shapes at home (most doors are rectangles, a window can be a square, a clock a circle) and a triangle drawn in the air. Match the Solids: all four solids beside their real things on the line the painting P17 already shows, a cylinder that rolls on its side and stands on its end, and rolling and stacking tried at home. More and Fewer: five fingers against two, snack plates, and lining two groups up one with one, where the group with some left over has more.

- Mikey committed through LU. This is the second half of First Steps' lessons and banks (pass LU did the first); the course's eighteen stories and its long story are next.
- Read against their standard. Both size lessons cite Texas Prekindergarten Guidelines V.D.1, which asks a child to compare heights or lengths of people or objects, and both taught only which thing takes up more room. Bigger and Smaller now teaches taller (towers that stand on the same floor) and longer (lines that start at the same place), and standing back to back with a friend to see who is taller (P114), and its questions now include the taller tower and the longer line, the kindergarten kinds, whose words the lesson now says. A cat between a mouse and a horse has its painting (P113). Big, Bigger, Biggest now says its own title's words, big, bigger, biggest, each one bigger than the one before (P115).
- Real sizes. A picture can show a bee and a bear the same size, so both size lessons now say so and name three groups: tiny (a bee, a snail), middle-sized (a cat, a rabbit, a duck, an owl, a fox) and huge (a bear, a whale) (P116). New kinds ask which of two animals is bigger or smaller in real life, and which of three is the biggest, the smallest or middle-sized. Only animals from different groups are compared, and a bear never meets a whale, since the smallest whales are about the size of a big bear. The setup line names the animals in alphabetical order and the pictures are shuffled on their own, so the bank counts each set of animals once; a first draft let the order vary, which counted every order as a new question and put Big, Bigger, Biggest at 369 when a child would meet 69.
- One, Two, Three. Its "How many?" kind had counted only to two in a lesson about three; a new kind asks one, two or three, dots or shapes. The lesson now counts on fingers and in claps, and says that things in a row or in a pile are each counted once. No painting, since a painted count could contradict the lesson.
- Patterns: a pattern with the body (clap, stomp, clap, stomp), beads on a string (P117), and one the child makes for a grown-up to guess. The three drawing lessons: lines in the world (rain falling in lines down, a table top across, lightning in a zigzag, P118, which takes that line off the picture-candidate list, now 32), each number said aloud on the way through the dots and the stars people joined with imagined lines to make pictures in the sky (P119), and the five shapes in real things (a button, a cracker, a slice of pizza, a card). Their banks are motor practice and stay as they are.
- Taking Turns names waiting as a feeling that can be hard and gives three things to do while you wait (a slow breath, counting to ten, cheering for a friend), with a swing to take turns on (P120). New kinds tell taking turns from sharing in a scene (one goes and then the other, or both at the same time) and choose what to do while waiting.
- Helpers All Around had no picture for the doctor, the teacher, the mail carrier or the police officer, and one line showed the firefighter, doctor and teacher chart while naming the mail carrier and the police officer. Each helper now has a line and a painting (P121 to P124), each says a little more (the fire truck, sick or hurt, reading stories, packages, cars on the street), two lines say where each helper works, and a last line says the child can be a helper too. New kinds ask who works where and which helper comes in a scene. The kindergarten courses share the old helper and good-choice kinds, so the new questions are kinds of their own and kindergarten's banks are unchanged.
- Banks: Bigger and Smaller 12 to 76 different questions, Big, Bigger, Biggest 9 to 69, One, Two, Three 20 to 36, Taking Turns 12 to 28, Helpers All Around 9 to 23; Patterns stays at 96. Eight new kinds, each re-derived in the rules test from its own words with tables the generators do not share; three were broken on purpose in a copy (the biggest and smallest swapped, a sharing scene called taking turns, the wrong helper at the post office), and the test failed on each. The new lesson lines and one practice round in each changed module were looked at in the real page at phone size: the towers stand together and the lines start together, each real-size question names its animals in a setup line the voice reads first, and the new paintings show their placeholders until Mikey makes them.

EARMARKS E12 places all 26 Approaches to Learning, Language and Communication, and Literacy goals (the Approaches to Learning goals, and the child's own talk, are a grown-up's or the classroom's), keeps only II.D.1's expressive half, people and events, and lists what Listen and Point now teaches and deliberately does not cite (P-MATH 4's first and second, P-MATH 10's spatial words, P-LC 7's sorting by color).
- Every finding below was read against its source before it was applied; where one was not applied, the reason is given.
- Round one, in parallel: the lesson brief (Listen and Point), the accuracy check (both courses' lessons and stories, and all 116 early-years experiments), the Wonder and game brief, the story brief (Very First Steps' twelve module stories), the story flow brief (eleven of them), the picture brief (both courses), and the screen and code briefs (Mikey's notes).
  - Lesson. Besides the citations above: Listen and Tap said "A pizza is round" over a drawn slice, "A bird has wings, so it can fly" (penguins and kiwis cannot), and named the moon and a cloud over a picture of the sun and a fish side by side, so nothing was up or down; it never said "listen to the word, then find its picture", its key idea's second half. Which One Is Different? showed two things where "different" means unlike the others, never sorted though it cited sorting, and drew the shape to match larger than its twin, which by its own size line made both choices different. Circle and Square defined a square by its corners alone and told a child that many windows are square. Every bank was mostly recall: Circle and Square's 16 were 4 tasks recolored, every round repeating one; Which One Is Different?'s 72 were one task re-dressed, always unlike in shape and color together; Listen and Tap had 10 and Animal Sounds 12, all naming what was just heard; A and B's explanations said the question back; and five of the course's eight generators had no re-derivation in the rules test. The fixes: a square is "four corners, and its four sides are all the same length", a little square and a square turned on its corner are still squares, and size does not change the shape (V.C.4); a ball rolls and a block does not; "Many plates are round like a circle, and some windows are square." Which One Is Different? shows rows of three, says different can be the color, the shape or the size, and sorts by color (V.E.1), with a reason on the apple line. Listen and Tap says "This is a slice of pizza. We cut a pizza into slices to eat it.", "A bird has wings, and most birds can fly.", shows the sun, the moon and the clouds up in the sky and then the sun stacked over a fish down in the water (P100 moves to that line), and ends "When you practice, listen to the word, then find its picture and tap it." Animal Sounds adds that hearing tells you what is near and which sound came first and which second. Eleven new question kinds, each with its re-derivation: the shape by its corners, the real thing round like a circle or with corners like a square, the same shape at another size or turn; the odd one out by color, by shape and by size alone; the one that does not go with a group sorted by color; a picture found by what the lesson says it does or where it is; up in the sky or down in the water; which animal came first or second; and one of two sounds heard at once. A and B explains by the letter's look. Bank sizes are at the end.
  - Accuracy, Listen and Point and Very First Steps: the bird, the pizza and the windows (above, the same fixes), and Two Shoes sent Lena and her dad out in one shoe each (now two pairs). Its suggestions taken: real animals make lots of sounds, a block "does not roll" (on a slope it slides) rather than sits still, "Many words name things" (not every word names a thing), the tree known by its trunk, and CS619 drawing Mike at three. Its notes on the stories (a three-year-old alone in tall grass, where ticks wait; a hot pizza; a quote not credited; a boy who went home alone) went into the story rewrites below.
  - Accuracy, the experiments: all 116 ideas for pre-K 3 to grade 2 read as a careful parent would, with AAP, CPSC, Poison Control, Shriners, CDC and FDA sources. Twenty-seven had to change (eight for pre-K 3, five for pre-K 4, three for kindergarten, six for grade 1, five for grade 2; pre-K 4's two copies of Rain in a Jar counted once): coins, a wine cork, buttons, a pebble, dried beans in a tub a child can open, and a small toy, for three-year-olds (the AAP's choking list and the CPSC small-parts cylinder); a bucket of water; vinegar in a dropper; latex balloons, a choking risk to age eight (AAP, CPSC); hot water, hot syrup and steam over a boiling pot (scalds, Shriners); peanut butter (an FDA major allergen, in schools); a paper pinwheel on a pin (the CPSC sharp-point rule, under eight); a child slicing vegetables; a bag of mold opened near a child (CDC); a parking lot (NHTSA); a bug looked at closely where fire ants live (Texas A&M AgriLife); "mark where the sun comes up" (looking at the sun); a seed's root that the idea said comes after its sprout (it comes first, UF/IFAS); an order of melting that depends on sizes and places; and an hour's watch in which a plant cannot be seen to grow, so it acts like the rock beside it (now a few days, and hands washed after the snail, CDC). About forty more small changes were taken. A safety line now heads the experiments (below).
  - Wonder and game. w-same-or-different's scientist ended "so the honest answer is both" on a screen that says no answer is right, and his short voice said the same; Chloe called a one-color picture a wall; Georgette had no faith of her own; Mike tested nothing; and the prompt, "Are you the same as your friend", assumed a friend. All rewritten (quoted below). In w-big-or-small, Mike's proposed rewrite ("so I would not take either one on trust") had a three-year-old doubt a grown-up's "too small", which is how a safety limit is said; it ships reworded. The game: Listen and Point owned Red and Blue, a sort by color it never taught, while Very First Steps' Red and Blue lesson teaches it word for word, so Red and Blue moves to Very First Steps, and Listen and Point gets a new game, Step on the Circles (path-circles, a circle-square deck: circles and squares in the same four colors, so only the shape moves the dot to the star). Found along the way: Catch the Hexagons (grade 1) had never drawn a hexagon, since every chip shape but a circle, a square and a diamond fell back to a triangle; SvgChip now draws the hexagon and the rhombus.
  - Story, Very First Steps. Ten of its twelve stories were rewritten so each teaches what its lesson does and what the printed book lists under it, with a real turn, a grown-up to say each rule, and no general fact in the narrator's voice; The Other Mitten (read whole after MA) and Two Plates stand. Two Balls became Two Buckets: Mia and Sam sort red balls and blue balls into two buckets with Mia's mom there, and nobody goes home alone. Like Me? became There You Are!: Little Fox, looking for her brother, takes an owl for him until she sees its big round eyes and no pointy ears, and when her brother comes, the same in ears, eyes and color, the owl names himself the odd one out (the old story matched a duckling by its peep, and had a hen and a goat the lesson never names). One Small Bed compares height side by side and length from the same end, with no "light". Splash: Grandpa draws 1 and 2 in the dirt, says to point to each duck and that the last number tells how many, and Nell counts moving ducks. The First Line: Kai starts in the middle and runs off the page, then Mom makes a dot at the top and says where to start (the old story celebrated starting anywhere and ended on an uncredited Paul Klee line). One, Two, Three became Dot to Dot: four dots joined out of order cross, and in order, by the numerals 1 to 4 Dad writes, they make a boat. Where Is the Frog?: Grandma finds Theo's yellow toy duck in the green grass at once and says why (the colors are different), so Theo hides his green frog there, and she cannot find it; then he sorts his bath toys by color. Pizza Corners: Diego skips a little triangle, Dad says big or little it is still a triangle, and the moral has three straight sides. Two Shoes: two pairs. May I, Please?: Gus and Mira, new names, with Miss Hazel there. No lead child's name repeats in the course.
  - Story flow, on the old stories: three even runs across page breaks and a few grown-up phrases; the rewrites replaced those versions, and the new text went to the flow check in round two.
  - Picture. Forty-one of Very First Steps' forty-eight story rows were the batch tool's (prompt = alt + style), so Leonardo, which never sees the paragraph, would get names, "the girl" with no age, "the yellow duck" with no toy, "dot one" against a ban on numbers, and counts with no check note. The ten rebuilt stories' forty rows were written by hand to the brief, and twenty more rows were rewritten as it proposed (among them P98's plate seen straight on as a full circle beside a truly square window, P99's one red apple among green ones all one size and plain green, and P92 and P127 with size check notes, P127 exactly two shoes), with ", sun" in the negative prompt of the color lessons' outdoor pictures.
  - Screen and code, on Mikey's notes: the tour's card 8 (above); What's new and the reminder out of sight in a page-tall frame; a replayed tour opening over waiting news; a read during a loop back counted as elective; Copy throwing the keyboard focus onto the page; and a build older than its source. - Round two, second reads by the same seven.
  - Lesson: the sorting line "When we sort, the things that are the same go together" stood over a red circle grouped with a red square, which the lesson's own "same" (look just alike) calls different, so it says "Let's sort by color. Things that are the same color go together.", and the key idea and The Apple Puzzle follow; "Tap the one we cut into slices to eat" could offer the fish or the bird, and "down in the water" the bird (a duck swims), now never; the tree line named branches the drawn tree does not show (and a palm has none), so "A tree grows tall, with a trunk."; and "When you hear two sounds, one comes first and one comes second" was false of two at once, so "When one sound comes after another, one is first and the other is second." From its suggestions: P16 is a red ball rolling alone (the block was named a line later); the growling bear never makes "two animals are near"; the odd color is never red against green, the most common color vision deficiency (MedlinePlus); Very First Steps' Triangles defines a square by its equal sides too (pass KH), and grade 1's Read the Word says "Many words name a thing, a color, a number or a shape" (pass KF); E12 quotes P-LC 7 whole and places P-MATH 10's second sentence (read again on headstart.gov). Recorded clips of these lessons, if any were made outside the repository, must be made again, since every line after an inserted one moved its clip key.
  - Accuracy: the new safety line said hot or deep water needs a grown-up, while a young child can drown in an inch or two (AAP), so it now reads "Read each idea through before you start, and keep a grown-up nearby. Young children do every idea with a grown-up beside them. Small things and balloons can choke a young child, and even an inch or two of water can drown one, so stay within arm's reach of any water and keep hot water in grown-up hands." (worded for every grade, the screen check's point); Splash's duck that "came down from the sky" was painted as a white farm duck, and most farm ducks cannot fly (National Geographic), so the newcomer is a wild mallard. Its correction to round one: the AAP lists raw apple pieces among foods to keep from children under four, and no pre-K 3 child eats a raw apple now (The Apple Puzzle sorts its apples instead). From its suggestions: "an owl may be near" (a daytime hoot is most likely a mourning dove, Audubon), the Sun and Moon Chart says "Each time you can see the moon, at night or in the day, draw it." (NASA: some nights it is up only by day), the bird feeder's seed has no nuts, Georgette ties three-year-old Mike's shoe, the shadow moved "because the sun seemed to move across the sky", a picnic sandwich is "almost a triangle", and Tooth in Soda uses a hard-boiled egg, shell on.

- Wonder edits, shipped under Mikey's MB rule and quoted for his later check. Since an educator's approval is kept by the question's id, they reach classrooms that already approved these questions (the open question in RULES-AUDIT section 11 now has a live case).
  - w-same-or-different, the prompt, was: "Are you the same as your friend, or different?" Now: "Are you and a friend the same, or different?"
  - Frederick (The Scientist), short, was: "Everyone is a little the same and a little different." Now: "Let's test it! Ask a friend their favorite food, and listen. Is it your favorite too?"
  - Chloe (The Artist), short, was: "Different is what makes a picture interesting." Now: "When I paint two friends, I look for what matches, and then for what does not."
  - Frederick, was: "Every person shares almost everything with every other person, and still no two are alike. Both things are true at once, so the honest answer is both." Now: "Before I answer a question like this, I collect evidence. Ask a friend about their favorite food, game and song, and listen closely to each answer. Make two lists, one for what matches and one for what does not, and see what your lists tell you."
  - Chloe, was: "A picture made of one color is a wall. Art needs sameness to hold together and difference to be worth looking at. Friendships are a lot like that." Now: "When I paint two friends, I look twice. The first time I notice what matches, the same muddy boots or the same big smile. The second time I notice what does not, and that is how each face ends up looking like nobody else."
  - Georgette (The Grandparent of Faith), was: "Old stories are full of friends who were nothing alike and loved each other anyway. The differences were usually the point of the story." Now: "My faith teaches me that every person is made with care, and that no two are made the same. So when I meet someone very different from me, I look for what I can learn from them, and I always find something."
  - Mike (The Skeptic), was: "You will notice ways you and a friend are different, and noticing is fine. Different does not mean better or worse. It just means not the same." Now: "The same in what way? You and a friend might laugh at the same jokes and go to bed at different times, so I check one thing at a time. I keep my answer in pencil, because friends grow and change. If anyone says different means better or worse, I ask them how they know."
  - w-big-or-small, Georgette, was (the approved text): "Old stories are full of small ones who did big things. Being small has never meant being unimportant, and every grandparent knows it." Now, as pass MA proposed: "The old stories I love, some of them from my faith, are full of small ones who did big things. I have always believed that being small never means being unimportant."
  - w-big-or-small, Mike, was (the approved text): "Grown-ups sometimes say you are big and sometimes say you are small. Both can be true at once. It is one of the first questions with more than one good answer." Now, not the wording pass MA proposed: "Grown-ups call you big one day and too small the next, and I used to wonder which one was true. Now I ask, big enough for what? Big enough to carry your plate is not the same as big enough to drive. It is one of the first questions with more than one good answer."
  - Standing under the rule, already live: w-big-or-small's theme (world) and Frederick's line there (pass MA), and w-early-lost-my-turn's brain-and-body line (pass LY).

## 2026-10-11 (pass MD): Mikey's notes on pinning, state history, the story as a reward and the lit letters; earmark E12 part one, the feelings lessons; numbered questions and checkpoint zips

- Mikey opened a new chat on October 9: "New chat for The Wise Human. Unzip the project, read docs/NEW-CHAT.md, docs/RULES-AUDIT.md, docs/EARMARKS.md, docs/INDEPENDENT-CHECKS.md and the latest DECISIONS entry, then continue. MC not committed this time" So the commit message keeps MC and adds MD, and continue meant MC's NEXT: pre-K 3's earmark E12 (the outcomes an app can teach first), then pre-K 4. With it came four notes, each word for word below with what it became. The chat hit a usage limit on October 9 after the round-one fixes and five of the seven second reads, and resumed on October 11 with four more notes (below); nothing was lost, since the workspace kept every file, but the stop is why checkpoint zips exist now.
- His first note: "Is there a way to Pin the screen for early learners?" The answer, given on October 9: no web page can lock a tablet by itself (browsers refuse it on purpose), so the device does the pinning: on an iPad or iPhone, Guided Access (Settings, Accessibility, Guided Access, a passcode; open the app and triple-click the top or side button, tap Start; triple-click again, the passcode, End; Apple's page of July 24, 2026), on Android, App pinning (Settings, search pin; open the app, swipe up and hold or tap Overview, tap the app's icon, Pin; Google's page, and on a Samsung Galaxy, Settings, Security and privacy, More security settings, Pin app), and in both cases the app added to the home screen first (Safari's Share menu, Add to Home Screen; Chrome on Android's menu, Install and create shortcut, then Install, since a plain shortcut opens in the browser), so the pin holds the app rather than a browser a child can type in. An in-app guide with those steps was built (a line in the add-student popup when Early years is chosen and a line under the walk-throughs on My Classroom, opening a pop-up ordered by the device in hand) and read by every check; on October 11 Mikey wrote "Let's remove the pin screen text that you were working on", and the guide, its two links, its device test, the idle-clock hold and its browser checks were removed whole (Q19 asks whether that reading was right). The steps above are the record of the answer.
- His second note: "Like Texas, can we also provide Historical information for each state depending on what state an educator selects when signing up?  We can earmark for after the grade reviews." Earmarked as program item L6 in docs/EARMARKS.md: the state is chosen once (at setup or with Change state) and today decides only which framework the map, transcript and printed book name; the history taught is Texas's (grade 4's The Story of Texas, grade 7's Texas History, Texas threads in the early grades); after the grade reviews, read each state's own social studies standards in full, write its history course at the full standard and show it in place of the Texas course, and give the early-grade threads each state's own facts. Reading the plans for it turned up two accuracy items: A18, five history plans cite 2018 editions of the social studies TEKS, while 19 TAC §§113.11 to 113.20 are "Adopted 2022", implemented from 2024-2025 (and, from the second accuracy read: new kindergarten to grade 8 social studies TEKS were adopted on June 26, 2026, with a grade 8 Texas history capstone, and high school ones on September 4, 2026, implemented from 2030-2031 in kindergarten to grade 5 through 2033-2034 in high school, so the 2022 sections stay cited until then and L6 reads the 2026 chapter when published); and A19, STATES in src/curriculum.mjs maps every state but Texas to the Common Core, though the National Center for Education Statistics' Table 2.17 (2015) lists Alaska, Nebraska, Texas and Virginia as never adopting it, Indiana, Oklahoma and South Carolina as reversing their adoption in 2014, Minnesota as English language arts only, and Florida's State Board of Education adopted its B.E.S.T. standards in its place on February 12, 2020 (classrooms from 2021-2022). The STATES comment says so now; the screens, which say matched to the Common Core State Standards rather than naming a state's own standards, are unchanged until each state's standards are read.
- His third note: "For your question about stories for early learners (answer to question 4).   They can play after the lesson as a reward like you mentioned." Built as the story as a reward, in src/logic.mjs (rewardStoryDue, heardModuleStories, HEARD_STORIES_SHOWN) and src/ui.jsx: in a read-aloud course (pre-K 3 to grade 2), the result screen of the first passed round of a lesson with a story (passed, four of five right first time, which opens the next lesson; the star waits for a second pass on another day, and "after the lesson" was read as after the passed round, Q20) says "You earned a story!" (spoken as the screen opens, once a round, with the card's own words first) and its big gold arrow becomes an open book (Hear your story). The book logs the story's first read (story_read, as a reader's lesson would log it; in a walk-through it goes in the log kept in memory, so a Wonder's return never offers the book twice) and opens the story in a read-aloud form: it reads itself aloud at the course's pace a moment after the page opens, with a back arrow, a round drawn speaker (a square while it reads) beside the snail and the hare, and one big gold arrow at the foot that rests while the voice reads and invites a tap once it stops, then carries on exactly where the round left off (readAloudNext: a due Wonder question, the next lesson, the next course or home, the way the result's own arrow would). A reward read is never counted as an elective reread (it is the first read; storyReading is cleared). Afterwards the story waits in an early learner's Let's Read, newest first and at most six, under a line that says the stories earned in lessons wait there too, each a gold book that breathes and reads the story again (its arrow then goes home); every story stays in the educator's Story Log and the printed book. While the lesson's reward is due on the round that finishes a whole course, the course's long story's line and Let's Read! wait, so a child is offered one story at a time (Q17 asks whether to chain the long story instead; Q18 asks about the six). A voice that goes quiet without reporting its end is ended by a watch after two quiet seconds, so the arrow never rests forever. Older students' lessons keep View story before practice, as before.

Decided: lit letters in the dark theme take a deeper gold, #A67A26 (LIT_LETTER_DARK in src/ui.jsx), 3.17 to 1 on the almond paper #EFE8DC, up from the 2.66 to 1 of the light palette's gold (B.gold, #B8862B), where large letters need 3; the light theme is frozen and keeps its gold (3.24 to 1 on white). The dark-contrast walk now measures a lit A on its paper, and fails unless the paper itself is the background it found (the screen check's second read: with the paper gone, the dark card passed at 3.6).
- Earmark E12 part one, the feelings outcomes, two new Very First Steps lessons after Please and thank you, each read in full on TEA's PK3 Streamlined Version and headstart.gov and quoted word for word in the plan and the sources lines:
  - Happy, sad, mad and scared (four-feelings, skill Feelings, order 13): a face can show how someone feels; a happy face smiles, a sad face turns its mouth down with a tear, a mad face squeezes its eyebrows down, a scared face opens its eyes wide; the body can show feelings too (mad can feel hot, with tight fists; scared can make the heart beat fast, and you may want to hide); every feeling is okay to have, even mad, hitting and pushing are not, because they hurt, when you feel mad use your words; say your feeling's name (I feel sad, I feel mad, I feel scared), and when a feeling is very big find your grown-up for a hug, a teddy to hold and a slow breath together, pretending to smell a flower and to blow out a candle. Cites PK3 I.B.2.a, I.B.2.b, I.B.2.c and ELOF P-SE 6, and P-SE 8 in part (a grown-up's help for a big feeling; for a smaller one, only its name and your words). Ten spoken lines, each with its picture: the faces are drawn by the screen (FeelingFace, a round yellow face so no child's own skin is the one drawn, one sign each; the scared face redrawn after the picture check so its worried eyebrows and wide open mouth read as fear, not surprise), with a face grid two to a row (an odd last face centered) and two paintings, P128 (two children laughing, faces toward the viewer) and P129 (a grown-up's hug and a slow breath).
  - Helping a friend (help-a-friend, skill Getting along, order 14, after four-feelings): faces can show feelings; when a friend looks sad or scared, be kind and ask, are you okay, sit beside them or bring a teddy; when a friend falls and gets hurt, or is very sad, get a grown-up; when two friends both want one ball and a fight starts, grabbing and pushing are not okay, keep your hands to yourself, say, stop, please, then get a grown-up, who can help you take turns. Cites PK3 I.C.5, I.C.6 in part (a friend who is distressed, not yet a grown-up who is), I.D.1 in part (noticing a friend's feelings and asking about them), and ELOF P-SE 5, P-SE 6 and P-SE 7. Eight lines, with the stop hand on the stop, please line and paintings P130 (a child leading a grown-up to a friend who fell) and P131 (turns with one ball).
  - Banks: ten new kinds (tap the named face; name the face shown; how a child in one of the lesson's own moments might feel, answered with a face, the wrong face happy, or sad when happy is right, never a feeling a child could fairly have there too; is it okay to feel sad, mad, scared, or to hit or push; who to find and what helps when a feeling is big, what to say when your face looks like this (the face shown and never named, the wrong choice another feeling's I feel), the flower and the candle; the friend who might need help (happy as the wrong face), or who looks sad or scared (another feeling's face as the wrong one, so the face must be read); the kind thing to say or do; the grown-up to get; the grab answered with stop, please, the fight with a grown-up, who helps you both get to play by helping you take turns; kind or not), each re-derived in tests/logic.test.mjs from its own tables, 26 and 19 distinct questions. A face choice (face:sad) is a picture, so it never speaks; describeChoice and askedNames name it.
  - Stories: The Big Boom (Nia, snug in bed with her teddy, hides under the blanket when far thunder follows a flash and the scared feeling grows; she remembers Dad's words, that feelings have names, like happy, sad, mad or scared, say its name and when it is big, call me; she calls, Dad says it is okay to feel scared, and they breathe slowly together, a flower in and a candle out, until her heart slows; moral: happy, sad, mad or scared, every feeling is okay, say its name, and when it is big, take a slow breath with your grown-up; 187 words) and One Ball, Two Friends (Owen and Tess pull one red ball at recess until it slips and Tess falls; Owen wants to grab it and run off, but looks at her face, kneels, asks are you okay, and runs to Miss Rae: we both pulled, and Tess fell, her hand hurts; Miss Rae finds the hand only a little sore, hugs Tess and tells them that when a friend is hurt, or you start to fight, get a grown-up, then helps them take turns; moral: look at a friend's face, and ask, are you okay, and when a friend is hurt, or you start to fight, get a grown-up; 199 words). Pictures S3882 to S3889, each written by hand with a check note where a count or a look matters, with each person given one look that holds across the story (Nia's curly brown hair and yellow pajamas, Dad's short brown hair and blue sweater, Owen's short black hair and blue shirt, Tess's two dark braids and purple shirt), night said in every bedroom scene, the bed across the room from the window (the National Weather Service: stay away from windows in a storm), no candle in the room, the hand held up, Miss Rae a woman, the ball on the grass; coloring pages D238 (a child hugging a teddy, a flower and a ball) and D239 (two children rolling one big ball); audio tags on every line ([distant thunder rumbling], [thud] Bump!, the morals [slowly, warmly]); 59 new clips in the audio ledger.
  - E12 narrowed: I.B.2.a, I.B.2.b, I.B.2.c and I.C.5 taught whole; I.C.6's distressed grown-up and I.D.1 beyond a friend's feelings stay listed; P-SE 6 and P-SE 7 off the Head Start list; P-ATL 1 is Head Start's own twin of P-SE 8 ("This is the same as P-SE Goal 8") so the grown-up's list starts at P-ATL 2, and P-ATL 4's gentle touches and friendly words are reminded of in both lessons (keep your hands to yourself; use your words) and not cited, since the goal is the child's growing habit. Part two, the rest of the teachable list, is next.

Left off, with the reasons in the code: Hands Are Not for Hitting (Martine Agassi; the board book is for ages 1 to 4, but its notes for grown-ups suggest venting a feeling out, yelling into a pillow and a mad dance with punches in the air, which the rule on hard feelings of pass IX keeps out), Glad Monster, Sad Monster (Hachette: ages 4 to 8) and Todd Parr's The Feelings Book (the picture book ages 4 to 6; its LB Kids board book of 2005 is listed from birth to 3, so it could join after a read of its pages).

  - One more and one fewer (one-more-one-fewer, Very First Steps, skill Counting, order 15, after More and fewer): two dots, touch each dot once as we count, the last number tells how many; one more dot comes and there are three, adding one makes more; one dot goes away and there are two, taking one away makes fewer; adding more than one makes more too (two more dots come, four dots) and taking more than one away makes fewer (two go away, two left), so V.B.1's and V.B.2's "one or more" is taught whole; one more each time up to five, counted to five; one away each time down to one; three dots are one more than two dots, two dots are one fewer than three dots, count each group to see; and at snack time one more cracker makes more, eating one makes fewer, try it, put two crackers on a plate, add one more and count them (the standard says a child uses objects, so the child is asked to). ### Q6: Two Plates takes its own trap ("another trap")
- Pre-K 4's The Long Row keeps the long row (three strawberries spread out against four in a bunch); pre-K 3's Two Plates now turns on size: three big crackers against five little ones. Ana points at the big crackers, wanting the plate with more crackers, Mom says "Big is not the same as more" and has her count each plate, touching each cracker once, and five little crackers are more than three big ones, so Ana takes the five and shares them with Mom. The story's more is a count: three big crackers, each twice as wide, are more cracker than five little ones, and the first version had Ana take the five as if they were more food (the alignment read). The second paragraph gives the sizes and not the answer (round one: it had said which plate had more before Ana counted). The moral is the key idea with the lesson's own spoken line: "Count each group to find which has more. Big is not the same as more. Fewer means not as many." 152 words, its audio rebuilt (the stories test holds the audio, tags stripped, to the words), its four pictures (S125, S126, S1379, S1380) rewritten by hand with one look for Ana and one for Mom and a check note counting three big and five little crackers, each big one about twice as wide.
- A story uses only what its lesson teaches, so More and Fewer teaches the trap first: a paragraph ("Big things can look like more too. Three big circles are still fewer than five little circles. Big is not the same as more, so count each group, whatever the size.") and two spoken lines, three big circles over five little circles ("The big circles look like more. Do they have more?", then the count and "Big is not the same as more."), stacked so the little circles draw large enough to count, the big row a little shorter than the little row so size is the only cue that misleads (a pair's half may keep its own frame since this pass). The lesson painting P126 moved from step 9 of the script to step 11, still the snack line, now the last. The bank still asks only more, fewer and the same number with dots of one size: counting to compare across sizes is placed at four and a half to five (Head Start's P-MATH 4 progression for 36 to 48 months compares objects of about the same size; North Carolina's foundations put different sizes at 54 to 60 months; Clements and Sarama at about five), so pre-K 3 models it, and pre-K 4's More and Fewer will ask it when its review comes (EARMARKS A7). More and Fewer gained an experiment as well, Big blocks, little blocks: three big wooden blocks and five smaller ones, every block too big to swallow, guessed and then counted (the alignment read). The accuracy check confirmed three-year-olds are misled by size (Rousselle and Noel 2008) and that counting is how to compare (IES practice guide, 2013).

### Q8: one style for lesson paintings, framed by what they show ("your choice")
- The first message said each lesson painting would take its subject's anchor, as story scenes do; reading the 134 rows changed the judgment. A lesson painting shows one real thing a lesson line names, and its course's subject often says nothing about the picture (P88's fire truck beside an apple sits in a math course, and "distinct geometric shapes" would stylize the truck). So every P row keeps the one house style, and its framing follows what it shows: a dynamic close-up for one thing; a straight-on view where a shape, a size or a length must read true (a close-up's perspective turns a circle oval and shrinks the far paper clips; 28 rows: the shapes beside real things, the coins, the ruler and the paper clips, the clock's hands, the sizes compared side by side, the rows of toys and the plates of crackers, the plate of portions, the keyboard, the moon's shapes and the bean's life); and a wide view where a whole landmark or place must show (12 rows: the Statue of Liberty, the Alamo, the Texas Capitol, the White House, Columbus's three ships, the animal homes, a town seen from above, the landscapes and the two houses, families at a park, the playground, and the mail carrier with the truck). Things that lie flat are seen from directly above. The straight-on rows said "a flat, straight-on view" until the alignment read, since flat can read as flat design beside the 3D style. The ledger test holds every P row to the three framings and fails a story anchor anywhere in one; that is his "professional yet fun and look sleek and modern yet relevant and educational" read as the house style kept and the subject drawn true.

### The read-along
- The light ("At least on dark theme, the highlighted text, while audio is playing, should be a light green background to see the highlighted words more clearly."; at 2:03, "I meant just the words (how they were before) but the highlight color is supposed to make it easier to read."): the light marks the sentence the voice is saying, in a story as on a lesson line. Before this pass a story lit its whole paragraph and a pre-reader's lesson line lit its sentence; the first build of this pass kept the paragraph, which his 2:03 note caught. speakSequence reports each sentence as it starts, a recorded clip's sentence is worked out from the time played, and RichText lights it (data-read-lit), hugging the words (LIT_WORDS: rounded at each line's ends, its padding taken back by a margin so the words never move), with the space after a sentence outside the light so it never runs into the next word (the screen check). In the dark theme it is the light green #AAD8C5 under the ink #16201B, 10.6 to 1; the light theme keeps its frozen gold tint (Q32 asks). The sentence is the finest step every device can follow: the browser's voice reports single words on some devices only, and the recorded clips carry no word timings yet, so a light that moves word by word is Q36.
- The snail and hare ("This icons would be better suited to the right of the title where the sound icon is closer to the same size as the fast and slow toggles. ... Not above the story card, within the card and to the far right.  Make sure the title stays true to center and isn't pushed left."): they sit inside the story card, to the right of the title, in a row whose empty left column matches the right one, so the title is truly centered (measured at 640 and 700 pixels), and the speaker is the size of the pace taps. The hare is redrawn as a rabbit silhouette ("which the rabbit should be redrawn to feel less like a stick figure and more like a rabbit silhouette").
- The pace ("the story should continue to read but the speed should adjust in real time.  Not stop the audio."): a tap on the snail or the hare keeps reading, starting the sentence in the voice's mouth again at the new pace (stop.setNudge), in a story and in the printed book's reader alike (BookReader, the screen check); two quick taps never start two readings (run tokens, the screen and code checks), and a tap on the pace already set does nothing.
- The scroll ("The stories, as they are being read and words are highlighted, pulls me back up the page when I scroll down and sit still."): the page follows the voice only until the reader scrolls (a wheel, a key, or a touch that moves 12 pixels, so a tap that wobbles does not count), and follows again once the voice reaches a paragraph on the screen. The browser check the alignment read asked for found one more way to be pulled back: a wheel or a finger in the first second after the reading started was taken for the page's own scroll and ignored. A wheel, a key or a finger now always counts as the reader, and only a bare scroll event waits out that second; question-screens holds it (a reader who scrolls down is not pulled back up when the voice moves to the next paragraph).

Can we make the images fill the space a little better even if more vertical space is needed (within reason)."; at 2:03, "Please make the answer choice buttons and corresponding images the size they were before and enlarge the lesson images instead."): the answer buttons and their pictures are exactly as before, and the question's own picture and the lesson pictures grow instead (Picture's big): 1.45 times from 700 pixels wide when the screen is at least 600 tall, 1.12 times on a phone at least 720 tall, and as before on a shorter screen, so Check answer stays above the fold on an iPhone SE and on a phone held sideways (the screen and code checks). ### The Wonder questions

This will affect multiple parts of the app.  Use your best design judgement."): all 94 early questions have four short voices, and a pre-reader hears Frederick, Chloe, Georgette and Mike, each on a card of its own, then the closing card (wonderPreReaderCards); the educator's panel and the click-through say four.

Chloe's mountain line is his word for word. After the Wonder check a writer gave 43 of Frederick's 46 bare facts a frame, cut Chloe's I love from 20 lines to 9 and Georgette's grandmother from 12 to 5, and took every Actually out of Frederick's mouth, since it sounded like correcting the child (108 lines in 69 questions, every other field checked unchanged). The Wonder check's second read then changed 41 more voices and three closings: eight lines it held must change (Mike's "The trick" right after Georgette's prayer, an "actually" in the middle of a line, a spill heard as the thing to make again), and 33 lines and the three closings it found worth changing (voices that made the same point, bare facts, words a three-year-old would hear wrongly, worn openings, and Frederick's "the sun does not go anywhere", strictly untrue since the sun orbits the galaxy). The second read of the late fixes then changed seven more lines a three-year-old hears once (the late reads, below). No short voice says actually now, which a rules check holds, Technically opens seven lines, Chloe's I love nine and Georgette's grandmother five. Every line is quoted below.
- The question above each voice ("They should also still see the question above what the characters are saying so they can remember what is being discussed.  It can be discrete."): a small, muted, italic line above each voice card (data-wonder-asked), 8.7 to 1 in the dark theme and 5.8 in the light.
- Portraits ("There should also be a face profile shot of the four characters answering the wonder questions." and his layout, name, then label, then picture, then the statement; "Let's create the prompts for the headshots."): every voice card shows the name at the top, the label under it, the portrait under both and the words below, 96 pixels wide on a pre-reader's card and 64 on a reader's. Leonardo prompts U2 to U5 (Frederick, Chloe, Georgette, Mike) are in ART-REQUESTS under Screen pictures, square, the head and shoulders with the sage-green background showing above the head and at both sides, checked at 64 pixels, each with its character sheet (C6, C4, C11, C2). Until a portrait is saved the app draws a stand-in, a friendly flat avatar in the style of his reference pictures, in the person's color with a small sign of how they see things (a flask, a palette, a heart, a question mark), wearing Mikey's note in a walk-through. Q33 to Q35 ask about their style, Frederick's age and the stand-ins' looks.
- The closing title ("The last ponder question should have a title above the text too.  Maybe it can actually rotate with titles that change ... You can add even more to the list so the titles feel adaptive and not overly repetitive although it is okay to repeat."): PONDER_TITLES in logic holds sixteen, his seven first (Let's Ponder!, Let's Reflect!, A Question for You, One More Thought, One Last Thought, One More, Here's One) and nine more (Your Turn to Wonder!, Think About This!, Wonder With Me!, Here's a Big One!, A Thought to Keep, Something to Wonder About, Ponder This!, Curious Minds Ask, Let's Think!; the alignment read swapped Food for Thought, an idiom a three-year-old hears literally when the title is read aloud). ponderTitle picks one from the question and the number of Wonder questions answered, so one visit always shows the same title and the next question another.
- The pondering pictures (his first note's "random images (that are animated like the title and fall into place from different directions in a playful way) surrounding the question"; "The let's wonder question should also be spiced up with icons around the question."; the 2:03 pictures; the 8:05 and 8:10 notes): PonderFrame is the card itself, on the Let's Wonder question and the closing card alike. Eleven pictures, six to a card: a child thinking with a finger at her chin and her eyes up at a cloud with a question in it, a figure meditating with a bun and a halo, hands pressed together and the face left blank, a globe on a stand, an idea bulb, a telescope, an atom's orbits, a pen writing on paper, an open book, a stack of books, a scroll and quill, and a question mark in a bubble. They are line art in the card's own ink at a little over half strength (4.3 to 4.7 to 1 in the dark theme, 3.35 to 3.5 in the light), with no fill, so the card shows through every shape; two or three sit in a band above the words (two, seven times in ten) and the rest in a band below, never beside the words, so the words keep the card's whole width; each has its own place, size (36 to 48 pixels on a phone, 46 to 64 from 700 pixels wide) and angle (up to 22 degrees either way), placed by its turned box so it never touches a word, and falls or rises in from the card's edge with a little bounce, then is still; with motion off it is simply there. The scatter comes from the question's id, so one question always looks the same and the next one different. The first build put the pictures around the card's outside in color; his 8:05 note moved them inside as line art, and the thinker and the meditator were redrawn from his pictures.

### More Info: why each wrong answer is wrong
- His note: "I wonder if it could be helpful to have explanations for each wrong answer too but it wouldn't clog up the screen.  The user would be able to select a discrete link that says "More Info"" and the four notes after it (quoted above).
- After an answer a quiet More Info button (data-more-info-link) opens a sheet (MoreInfoSheet): the question's own picture at the top, so "this one" and "these" point at something; then why each wrong choice does not fit (Why not the others?), the one just tapped first; then why the answer fits (Why this one fits); then more right examples (More right answers). It opens by itself after a reader's wrong answer, and is a button after a right one; for a pre-reader the button sits under the next button, since it is for the grown-up beside the child (the alignment read). Every sheet has a Read it to me speaker, so a pre-reader can hear it. More Info is a quiet text button that opens a sheet inside the app, not a link in the sense of CLAUDE.md's rule 7, which keeps out addresses that leave the app.
- The smart words come from the child's own record (choiceHistory and whyNotClause in logic): "which you just chose" for this tap, "which you chose once before too" when the child also tapped it on one earlier visit to this very question, and "which you have chosen a few times now" after two or more; a wrong choice tapped only on earlier visits reads "which you chose once before", or "which you have chosen before" after two or more (the same question made again from its seed, a reset or the lesson's own reset clearing the history; the code check). The first build said "last time", which is not true when the earlier visit was not the last one (the code and lesson checks); "once before" is Mikey's own phrase.
- A pre-reader's wrong taps before the right one are kept with the result (missed), only choices the question offered, so a later visit can say once before (missedPicks; the code check's first finding was that a failed tracing would have been stored there, and it never is).
- A pre-reader hears the reason after a wrong tap, then "Have another try." (preReaderWrongWords), so the explanation reaches a child who cannot open the sheet. A reason is held back, and the child hears "Not that one. Have another try.", only while two or more choices are still open and the reason names something of the answer the question has not said itself (a voice must never answer a retry for the child, RULES-AUDIT's rule since pass MC). The screen check found reasons that name the answer (87 of the 320 wrong taps it sampled), and the first rule held back every reason that did, 829 of pre-K 3's 1,529 distinct lines; the lesson check's second read found that left six lessons with no spoken reason at all, though in a two-choice question only the answer is left and most of the rest only repeat what the question asked ("you are looking for the cloud"), so now twelve four-color reasons are held back ("this one is yellow like a banana"); Q31 asks whether to say those too.
- Content: pre-K 3's 70 choice kinds, both courses, have a reason for every wrong choice (whyNot) and, in 69 of them (all but p3-tap-picture), more right examples (alsoRight), written from the lessons' own words; 35 older kinds, from grade 2 to college, show their choice notes as plain sentences; the other 1,394 choice kinds show no More Info yet (EARMARKS L10).
- The older kinds' sentences read as broken English until the alignment read caught them ("The southern colonies, which you just chose, is not the answer here. The southern colonies: big farms and slavery."): the sentence now says "cannot be the answer here", which agrees with a plural name, each note starts with a capital, and the 26 notes that were fragments around a colon are sentences now ("The southern colonies had big farms and slavery.", "Rewrote would mean made again from the start."), so a reader's sheet never shows the app's grammar slipping; a rules check reads every row of every sheet over 120 seeds of each kind for a capital at the start of each sentence and no colon. A worded answer's name above Why this one fits is capitalized too.
- The sheet on a phone: its top can always be scrolled to (the screen check found a tall sheet opening above the screen), a worded choice longer than three letters has no box, decided once for the whole sheet so Gas never sits in a box while Solid does not, a worded answer is named above Why this one fits, focus goes to Got it without scrolling the sheet, Escape closes it and focus returns to the link (the screen and code checks).
- His question, "I'm surprised that hasn't been a suggestion from you since one of your roles is educational expert.", deserved a plain answer: he is right. Feedback that explains why an answer is wrong, rather than only saying so, is among the best-supported moves in the research on feedback (Shute, 2008, Review of Educational Research), and no pass had proposed it. The lesson brief now asks that every wrong choice have a reason, said against the answer in the lesson's own words (item 7).

### Questions as one sentence
- His note: "The title, and others like it, that reads: What is a kind thing to do?  New line Your friend looks sad."  Would reach much better like What is a kind thing to do when your friend looks sad?  I thought we had a bot working on the questions' conversational tone?  Even for early readers"
- Pre-K 3's 37 situation questions, in seven kinds, ask one sentence now ("What is a kind thing to do when your friend looks sad?"), every old setup's facts kept (the lesson check read all 37 aloud). Everywhere else the setup line now sits above the question, the order the voice already speaks and Quick fire already shows; before this pass it sat under the prompt, the order pass IA chose with Mikey ("Setup lines", CLAUDE.md), so Q30 asks him. Merging the rest where one sentence reads better is EARMARKS L11 (872 kinds can still show a setup line, 770 of them on every question they ask). The alignment read added a line beside every place that still describes the old order (DESIGN.md, docs/QUESTION-REVIEW.md and tools/question-review.mjs), so no later pass takes the new order for a bug before Mikey answers.
- The honest answer about the bot: the writing review has read every pre-K 3 bank, but pass IA's rule kept a setup line apart under a prompt that made sense alone, so the split was kept on purpose and nobody asked whether one sentence would read better. The lesson brief asks that now.

### Mikey's words for the long row
- "Three dots, when spread far apart, create a row that appears long.  Five dots, when close together, create a row that appears short.  The long row looks like more.  Is it more?" is More and Fewer's spoken line 7 word for word (counting from 0, as the audio ledger's keys do: more-or-fewer-7), each sentence lit as it is said, and the size trap's line 9 is written in his style: "Three circles, when drawn big, take up lots of room. Five circles, when drawn little, take up only a little room. The big circles look like more. Are they more?"
- The long row's three dots are 74 apart, so the row is 250 pixels long against the short row's 182 (the lesson check: 18 percent longer did not "appear long"; its second read found that 90 apart shrank the long row's dots below the short row's on a 360-pixel phone, which would be a size cue).

### A long story at the first finish and again at mastery
- His notes: "I saw an arrow and not an unlocked long story"; "I think we need long stories for both the first full completion of a lesson (before mastery) and when they do it again on another day for mastery.  More stories are good and it is kind of a standout feature of The Wise Human.  The conversational tone and intricate interwoven storyline that blends into the features."; "Even for early readers, they should be launched into the long story at the end of a completed course (both 1st and 2nd time on different days)".
- Why he saw an arrow: a course's long story opened only with its last star, and a star needs a second passed round on another day, so the round that first passed every lesson ended on the usual arrow.
- A course now celebrates twice. The first time every lesson has been passed once (courseCompletedBy: the round whose pass completes the course; a Quick Review's clear fresh try on a lesson moved past and never passed counts; a lesson placed by a quick check or starred by a review does not, since placing is not doing every lesson, and a course completed by placing opens its long story on the shelf without a party) is the stage complete; the round that earns every star (courseFinishedBy) is the stage mastered (courseCelebrationStage). Both launch readers and pre-readers alike into a long story: the first opens the course's long story, the second its next long story (MASTERY_STORIES), or, while a course has none, the first again, said as again only once it was read. The words follow the stage (courseFinishedWords(course, stage)): "Hooray! You did every lesson in Very First Steps!" (passed every lesson, for a reader) and then "Hooray! You earned every star in Very First Steps!"; from grade 6, "Well done. You passed every lesson in" and "Well done. You finished" and the course's name.
- Both stories reach every place a long story goes: the shelf (longStoryRows; a young learner sees the open ones only), the Story Log, the printed book, the report's counts and elective reads, the audio ledger, the art, flow, length and age tools, and the review ledger (mastery-story:<id>, listed for every course since the final read, so the 120 still to write show as undone rows). A reader's Let's Read says, under the course stories' line, "Mastering every module unlocks the course's next story.", and a next story's row reads "the next story" with "N modules to master" until it opens.
- When Mikey chose Write both now: The rainy-day picnic (Very First Steps, CS631 to CS636, 458 words in nine paragraphs) brings the picnic indoors on a stormy day: Chloe sets the cups out in a long row and thinks there are more cups than friends, the thunder scares Mike and Frederick asks if he is okay, Miss Hazel has them breathe slowly and then count each group, three cups turn out to be fewer than four friends, and Mike fetches one more. The ball over the wall (Listen and Point, CS637 to CS642, 453 words in nine paragraphs) sends Mike's red ball over a wall: a thump and a meow tell him a cat is near, the letters A and P on a gate's sign say apple garden, and among the red apples his ball is the big one ("different can be size too"); ball and wall rhyme on the way home. A second long story for every other course is EARMARKS L9.
