- Pre-K 4's pattern questions (pp-what-next, pp-which-repeats and pp-missing: "What comes next?", "Does this repeat the same way each time?", "Which one is missing?") named their color `color`, which the drawing never reads, so every such row was drawn green whatever its answers' color; it is `colour` now, and the check can fail (the code check).
- A scripted rewrite of the short voices dropped the long voices of 40 early questions, caught before any check ran and restored from a snapshot; every field but the short voices was then compared with the snapshot (a rule for future passes: after a scripted rewrite of data, compare every other field).
- A finished tracing kept its strokes as the answer given in the log, older than the pass (the code check's second read); a result now keeps only traced or not traced, and the scripts test reads the source for it.
- Pre-K 3's "How might ... feel?" set happy as the wrong face in five of its six moments, older than the pass (the lesson check; EARMARKS A23, closed now at the alignment read's word): Rosa's thunder and Mia's fast heart are set against mad, Kai's hot face and fists against sad, and a lost balloon and a grabbed toy keep happy, since sad and mad both fit them; the rules test names the fair wrong faces of each moment and holds happy to at most half.
- Georgette's stand-in portrait looked younger than Frederick's (the alignment read), so it has a silver streak and smile lines now, her auburn hair kept from the canon (Q35 asks about the stand-ins' looks).

### Every Wonder line this pass changed (quoted for Mikey's later check, his rule since pass MB)
- 94 of the 366 Wonder questions changed, all of them early questions a pre-reader can meet; no reader-only question and no long voice (the four perspectives a reader sees) changed. Generated from the code before and after the pass (the scratch tool wonder-block.mjs; tools/wonder-changes.mjs, kept in the project since the final read, prints the same changes), so nothing is left out.
- Questions, choices and closings, old then new (8):
  - w-turned-square: its closing "What else stays the same when you turn it around?" became "Turn a block or a cup around. Is it still the same thing?" (the Wonder check: "turn it around" named nothing).
  - w-sleep-night: its choices At night, Because it is dark and Not sure became Because it is dark, Because we are tired and Not sure (found while the pass was built: "At night" did not answer a why question).
  - w-angry-feeling: the question "When you feel angry, where do you feel it in your body?" became "When you feel mad, where do you feel it in your body?"; its closing "What is one thing that helps your body calm down when it is angry?" became "What is one thing that helps your body calm down when you feel mad?" (the Wonder check: mad is the word pre-K 3's feelings lessons use, as pass MG did for cross).
  - w-hard-is-good: its closing "What is something that is hard right now? What is one small piece of it you can already do?" became "What is hard for you right now? What small piece of it can you already do?".
  - w-ocean-deep: its closing "If you could go to the bottom of the sea in a little window boat, what would you hope to see?" became "In a little window boat at the bottom of the sea, what would you hope to see?".
  - w-same-or-different: its closing "What is one thing that is the same about you and a friend, and one thing that is different?" became "What is one way you and a friend are the same, and one way you are different?".
  - w-fish-home: the question "A fish needs water and a bird needs a tree. What does your home give you?" became "A fish needs water, and many birds need trees. What does your home give you?" (the accuracy check: some birds, the killdeer among them, nest on bare ground).
  - w-ants-elephant: the question "Is a big group of tiny ants more than one elephant, or less?" became "Which is more, a big group of tiny ants or one elephant?"; its choices More, Less and It depends became The ants, The elephant and It depends (found while the pass was built: the lessons say fewer, never less, and the choices now name the groups).
- The short voices a pre-reader hears, all 94 early questions: before this pass two voices (as pass LY wrote them), now all four in the order heard, Frederick, Chloe, Georgette and Mike (Mikey: "We can also use all four voices, even for the early learners."). In w-big-or-small, Chloe's line is Mikey's word for word and Frederick's opens with his Technically. The text below is what ships (the checks that shaped it are under The checks, in layers):
  - w-favourite-colour ("Which color makes you happiest?"). Before, Chloe: "Every color is somebody's favorite." Frederick: "Your eyes see colors. Your heart picks one." Now, Frederick: "From what scientists know, your eyes see a color, and your brain decides how it makes you feel." Chloe: "To me, a favorite color is like a hug you can see." Georgette: "Red has always made me happiest. That is why I wear my red coat everywhere!" Mike: "My favorite color changes all the time. I wonder if yours will change too."
  - w-biggest-number ("Is there a biggest number of all?"). Before, Frederick: "Whatever number you say, you can always add one more." Chloe: "Try to draw the biggest number. You will run out of paper first." Now, Frederick: "I study numbers, and they never end. There is a special word for that, infinity!" Chloe: "I once drew dots for the biggest number. My paper ran out, but the numbers never did!" Georgette: "I believe kindness is like numbers. No matter how much you give, there is always more." Mike: "How would we check for a biggest number? If someone says they found it, I just add one!"
  - w-turned-square ("If you turn a square so it stands on a corner, is it still a square?"). Before, Frederick: "Turn a square tile any way you like. It still has four equal sides and four square corners." Chloe: "Standing on a corner it looks like a diamond. Looks can trick you, so count the sides." Now, Frederick: "I measured a turned square once. It still had four equal sides and four square corners." Chloe: "When I paint a square on its corner, it looks like a diamond. I still count four sides!" Georgette: "I believe people are like that square. Turned around by a hard day, we are still ourselves." Mike: "Trace a square block, then turn your paper. Did the square change, or only the way it sits?"
  - w-story-true ("Can a story be true and made up at the same time?"). Before, Chloe: "A made-up story can still tell you something true." Frederick: "The dog in the story is not real. The feeling might be." Now, Frederick: "From what I know, a made-up bee story can still teach true things, like how bees make honey." Chloe: "A pretend story can still make me cry real tears. That is my favorite thing about stories." Georgette: "I taught history for forty years. I loved the true old stories and the made-up ones too." Mike: "I ask two things about every story. Did it really happen, and does it feel true?"
  - w-who-made-the-rule ("Who made the rules at your house?"). Before, Frederick: "Rules are made by people, so people can talk about them and change them." Chloe: "The best rules are the ones you would make yourself if you were in charge." Now, Frederick: "I once counted the rules at my house. There were five, and each kept somebody safe or happy." Chloe: "A kind house rule feels warm to me, like everybody helping clean up after dinner." Georgette: "Our house had one rule I still keep today. Always tell the truth." Mike: "I wonder who made each rule at my house. Asking why, nicely, is always fair."
  - w-need-or-want-really ("Is a friend a need or a want?"). Before, Frederick: "People need other people. Even grown-ups get sad when they are alone too long." Chloe: "A friend is not food or a coat, but it is very hard to be happy without one." Now, Frederick: "I have read that people with good friends are often healthier and happier." Chloe: "When I am with a friend, colors look brighter and songs sound sweeter." Georgette: "In my long life, good friends have mattered as much as a warm supper." Mike: "I used to think friends were just for fun. Now I could not do without mine."
  - w-losing-the-vote ("Your class voted, and your choice lost. How does that feel?"). Before, Frederick: "Losing a vote feels bad for a while. Getting to vote again next time makes it fair." Chloe: "Sometimes the thing you did not pick turns out to be good too." Now, Frederick: "I count votes carefully. The choice with the most hands wins, and next time, everyone votes again." Chloe: "I think the thing you did not pick can still surprise you and turn out lovely." Georgette: "In forty years of teaching, I saw that being kind about losing makes a happy class." Mike: "Does losing a vote mean your idea was bad? Not always. Good ideas lose votes too!"
  - w-sky-blue ("Why is the sky blue?"). Before, Frederick: "Sunlight has every color in it. The air scatters the blue bits all over the sky." Chloe: "At sunset, the same sky turns orange and pink." Now, Frederick: "It turns out sunlight hides every color, and the air bounces the blue all around the sky." Chloe: "When I paint the sky, I mix lots of blues, and pinks and oranges for the evening." Georgette: "My grandmother called the sky her big blue blanket. I have loved that ever since." Mike: "I used to think the sea made the sky blue. But deserts have blue skies, and no sea!"
  - w-share-fair ("If you have three cookies and two friends, what is the fair way to share?"). Before, Frederick: "Three cookies, three people. One each is exactly equal." Chloe: "Fair does not always mean the same. It means everyone feels okay." Now, Frederick: "Count with me. You and two friends make three people, and three cookies make one each." Chloe: "To me, fair is when every face at the table is smiling." Georgette: "When I was little, we shared everything with our cousins. A shared treat tasted sweeter somehow." Mike: "Let's ask your friends what feels fair to them. They might surprise you!"
  - w-dreams ("Where do dreams come from?"). Before, Frederick: "Your brain keeps working while you sleep. Dreams are some of that work." Chloe: "Dreams mix up your day into new pictures. That is a kind of art." Now, Frederick: "From what scientists know, your brain stays busy while you sleep, and dreams come from that busy work." Chloe: "Dreams are like paintings my sleepy brain makes at night, with no brushes at all!" Georgette: "I taught my students about a dream book from Egypt. It is over three thousand years old!" Mike: "Even today, nobody knows for sure what dreams are for. I love a mystery we are still solving!"
  - w-sleep-night ("Why do we sleep at night and not in the day?"). Before, Frederick: "Your body has a clock inside. It feels sleepy when it gets dark." Chloe: "Night is quiet. Quiet is good for dreaming." Now, Frederick: "From what scientists know, your body has a little clock that makes you sleepy when it gets dark." Chloe: "Night feels soft and quiet to me, like the whole world is tucking in." Georgette: "At bedtime I say a quiet prayer. It tells my heart the day is done." Mike: "I wonder about owls. Most of them sleep in the day and hunt at night!"
  - w-rain ("Where does rain come from?"). Before, Frederick: "Water goes up into the sky as tiny bits, then falls back down as rain." Chloe: "Rain is the sky giving the water back." Now, Frederick: "Did you know clouds are full of tiny water drops? When they grow heavy, down comes the rain!" Chloe: "I think rain on the roof sounds like tiny drums. I could listen all day." Georgette: "I like to say a little thank-you for rain. It helps the gardens grow." Mike: "Why not the clouds and the sea? Water goes round and round, from sea to cloud and back."
  - w-animals-talk ("Do animals talk to each other?"). Before, Frederick: "Animals do not use words, but they tell each other things with sounds and moves." Chloe: "A wagging tail says a lot without any words." Now, Frederick: "It turns out honeybees dance to tell each other where the flowers are." Chloe: "My own dog's wagging tail is my favorite hello, and it does not need one single word." Georgette: "Old stories from all over the world have talking animals. I have loved them since I was small." Mike: "Some parrots can say hello. But do they know what hello means? I wonder!"
  - w-leaves ("Why do leaves change color in the autumn?"). Before, Frederick: "The green fades away in autumn, and the yellow and red were hiding underneath." Chloe: "Autumn is when the trees show all their colors at once." Now, Frederick: "I once tested a green leaf and found yellow hiding inside. In fall, the green fades away." Chloe: "I think fall is when trees put on their party clothes, red, orange and gold." Georgette: "Every fall, I watch the trees let go of their leaves so gently. It always calms me." Mike: "I wonder why some trees stay green all winter. So it cannot be just the cold!"
  - w-bigger-better ("Is bigger always better?"). Before, Frederick: "An elephant is big, but an ant can carry more than its own weight." Chloe: "A small picture can say more than a big one." Now, Frederick: "Technically, an elephant is huge, but it cannot climb a tree. A little squirrel can!" Chloe: "I love tiny drawings. You hold them close, and they feel like a secret." Georgette: "My favorite old story is the tiny mouse who saves the big lion." Mike: "Better for what? A giant spoon would never fit in your mouth!"
  - w-friend ("What makes a friend a friend?"). Before, Frederick: "Friends are people who spend time together and look after each other." Chloe: "A friend is someone you can be quiet with." Now, Frederick: "From what I have seen, friends spend time together and look after each other." Chloe: "I think a friend is someone you can be quiet with, and it still feels cozy." Georgette: "I believe kindness is the glue that holds friends together. My oldest friends are my kindest." Mike: "Can a puppy be a friend? Lots of people would say yes!"
  - w-music-move ("Why does music make us want to move?"). Before, Frederick: "Your body hears the beat and wants to keep time with it." Chloe: "Music is a feeling you can hear. Moving is how it gets out." Now, Frederick: "I once watched babies wiggle to music, all on their own. A beat seems to tug at us!" Chloe: "When I dance, the music tells my feet what to do. I just follow along!" Georgette: "At family weddings, young and old dance side by side. Music brings my whole family together." Mike: "I wonder why some people wiggle and others sit still. Maybe bodies feel music differently."
  - w-brave-scared ("Can you be brave and scared at the same time?"). Before, Frederick: "Brave is what you do. Scared is what you feel. You can do both at once." Chloe: "The bravest people in stories are scared first." Now, Frederick: "Technically, scared is a feeling, and brave is something you choose to do." Chloe: "In every story I love, the hero is scared first. Then they do the brave thing anyway." Georgette: "When I feel scared, I say a little prayer, and then I take one brave step." Mike: "I used to think brave people never felt scared. Then I asked, and they all felt scared too!"
  - w-smallest ("What is the smallest thing you can think of?"). Before, Frederick: "Everything is made of bits far too small to see." Chloe: "Try drawing something so small the pencil is too big." Now, Frederick: "I checked once under my microscope. One drop of pond water was full of tiny living things!" Chloe: "I draw tiny things big, like a seed that fills my whole page." Georgette: "A ladybug on my finger fills me with wonder. There is so much life in something so small!" Mike: "People once thought they had found the smallest thing. Then they found even smaller bits inside it!"
  - w-fell-off-bike ("When you fall off a bike, what should you do next?"). Before, Frederick: "Everyone who can ride a bike fell off first. Falling is part of learning." Chloe: "It is okay to cry, and then get back on." Now, Frederick: "It turns out each try teaches your body more balance, even the falls!" Chloe: "To me, a fall stings twice, on your knee and in your heart. Both get better." Georgette: "When I learned to ride, I fell more times than I can count, and I kept going." Mike: "Before I get back on, I ask what went wrong. Then I try again a little slower."
  - w-got-it-wrong ("You tried a question and got it wrong. Is that bad?"). Before, Frederick: "A wrong answer shows you what to learn next. That is useful." Chloe: "Every drawing I love came after a lot of ones I threw away." Now, Frederick: "In my lab, I get things wrong every day. Each wrong answer points me somewhere new." Chloe: "My favorite drawings came after lots of ones I crumpled up. Wrong ones are practice!" Georgette: "In forty years of teaching, I loved wrong answers. They showed me what to teach next." Mike: "Is a wrong answer bad? I am not so sure. I always ask why it was wrong."
  - w-try-again ("Why does trying again usually work better than trying the first time?"). Before, Frederick: "The second time, you already know one thing that does not work." Chloe: "The second try has the first try inside it." Now, Frederick: "My experiments go better the second time. By then, I know one way that does not work!" Chloe: "I think every new try has the old tries tucked inside it, like layers of paint." Georgette: "My grandmother made bread every week. She said her hands got a little wiser each time." Mike: "I used to try the very same way again. Now I change one little thing first."
  - w-angry-feeling ("When you feel mad, where do you feel it in your body?"). Before, Frederick: "Angry feelings show up in the body first: hot face, tight hands, fast heart." Chloe: "If anger had a color and a shape, what would yours look like?" Now, Frederick: "If you measure it, a mad feeling can make your heart beat faster and your face feel hot." Chloe: "When I am mad, I picture it as a red, spiky shape. Naming its color helps me." Georgette: "I often feel mad in my tummy first. A slow breath helps it settle." Mike: "My mad feeling starts in my hands. I wonder where yours starts, and if it moves."
  - w-sad-okay ("Is it okay to feel sad?"). Before, Frederick: "Sad is a normal feeling. It comes, and then it goes." Chloe: "Some of the most beautiful songs are sad ones." Now, Frederick: "Here is something true. Everyone feels sad sometimes, and sad feelings come and go." Chloe: "I think some of the most beautiful songs are sad ones. Sad can be lovely too." Georgette: "I still feel sad sometimes, even at my age. A cup of tea and a hug help me." Mike: "I used to hide sad feelings. Then I tried telling a friend, and I felt lighter. Try it!"
  - w-name-feeling ("Why does it help to say what you are feeling out loud?"). Before, Frederick: "Naming a feeling makes it a little smaller and easier to hold." Chloe: "A feeling with a name is a feeling you can do something with." Now, Frederick: "When scientists tested it, saying a feeling's name helped people feel a little calmer." Chloe: "A feeling with no name is like a shape in the dark. A name turns on the light." Georgette: "My mother asked me every night, how is your heart today? Saying it out loud helped." Mike: "Need a feeling word? Point to where you feel it, and a grown-up can help you find one."
  - w-bad-day ("Everyone has bad days. What makes a bad day end?"). Before, Frederick: "Every day ends, and a new one starts. Bad days do not last forever." Chloe: "Even a gray day has a little bit of color in it somewhere." Now, Frederick: "Scientists found that missing sleep makes people less happy and more worried. Sleep matters on a bad day!" Chloe: "Even a gray day has one bright color somewhere, like a red umbrella or a yellow cup." Georgette: "In my long life, every bad day has ended, and a new morning has come." Mike: "I kept a list of my bad days. A week later, most of them felt much smaller."
  - w-everyone-struggles ("Does everyone find some things hard?"). Before, Frederick: "Everyone finds some things hard. Even grown-ups. Even experts." Chloe: "The people who look like it is easy have just practiced a lot." Now, Frederick: "Everyone does, even grown-up scientists. I still find whistling very hard!" Chloe: "The people who make it look easy have usually practiced a lot. I practice every day." Georgette: "In forty years of teaching, I never met one child who found everything easy. Not one." Mike: "Only me? I tested that once by asking around. Lots of people found the same things hard."
  - w-things-change ("Some days feel great and some feel awful. Is that normal?"). Before, Frederick: "Feelings go up and down like waves. That is how they are meant to work." Chloe: "A song with only one note would be boring. Ups and downs are the music." Now, Frederick: "From what scientists know, everyone's feelings go up and down like waves, even mine!" Chloe: "I think a song with only one note would be so boring. Ups and downs make the music." Georgette: "My faith reminds me that hard days and happy days both pass, like seasons." Mike: "I like to keep a bad day the size of one day, and not let it grow."
  - w-slow-learner ("Is it bad to learn something slowly?"). Before, Frederick: "Slow learning often lasts longer than fast learning." Chloe: "A tree grows slowly. Nobody says a tree is bad at growing." Now, Frederick: "I study how people learn. A little each day helps you remember more than rushing." Chloe: "A tree grows slowly, and nobody says it is bad at growing. I love slow things." Georgette: "I still smile at the tortoise and the hare. Slow and steady won the race!" Mike: "Who says learning slowly is bad? A slow reader might be a super fast swimmer!"
  - w-birds-fly ("How do birds fly?"). Before, Frederick: "Wings push the air down, and the air pushes the bird up." Chloe: "Watch a bird land. It is the most careful thing you will see all day." Now, Frederick: "Technically, wings push the air down, and the air pushes the bird up." Chloe: "I love watching a bird land. It slows down, spreads its tail, and stops just right." Georgette: "Long ago, people could only dream of flying like the birds. Now we have airplanes!" Mike: "I wonder if a bird could fly with no feathers. It could not, so feathers matter too!"
  - w-shadow ("What is a shadow?"). Before, Frederick: "A shadow is the place where you are blocking the light." Chloe: "Shadows change shape all day. Try tracing yours." Now, Frederick: "I test shadows with a flashlight. A shadow is the spot where my hand blocks the light." Chloe: "Shadows are my favorite thing to paint. They make a picture look round and real." Georgette: "As a girl, I made my shadow dance on my bedroom wall. I called it my little friend." Mike: "Can a shadow disappear? In a room with no light at all, it does. No light, no shadow!"
  - w-why-wash-hands ("Why do we wash our hands?"). Before, Frederick: "Tiny living things too small to see live on your hands. Soap washes them off." Chloe: "Warm water and bubbles is a small nice thing you can do every day." Now, Frederick: "Under my microscope, I have seen tiny germs. Soap and water wash them right off your hands!" Chloe: "Warm water and bubbles feel so cozy to me. Washing my hands is a happy little moment." Georgette: "My mother made us wash before every supper, long before I knew about germs." Mike: "How do we know washing works? Scientists tested it, and fewer people got sick!"
  - w-worried-first-day ("Is it normal to feel worried before something new?"). Before, Frederick: "Everyone feels wobbly before something new. Your body is getting ready." Chloe: "The wobble means you care about it." Now, Frederick: "Here is how it works. A fluttery tummy before something new is your body getting ready." Chloe: "Before every art show, I feel wobbly inside. To me, the wobble means I care." Georgette: "When I was little, I stood at the school door, so worried. Then I walked in anyway." Mike: "I like to ask what exactly I am worried about. Saying it out loud often shrinks it."
  - w-jealous ("What does it feel like when a friend gets something you wanted?"). Before, Frederick: "That mixed-up feeling has a name: jealous. Everyone gets it." Chloe: "You can feel jealous and still be glad for your friend, at the same time." Now, Frederick: "I feel jealous sometimes too, even as a grown-up scientist. Everyone does." Chloe: "I think a heart can hold two things, glad for your friend and wishing you had one too." Georgette: "I remember feeling jealous of my cousin's red bike. The feeling passed, and we rode it together." Mike: "I check what I really want. Is it the toy, or a turn? Often a turn is enough."
  - w-say-sorry ("Why is it hard to say sorry, and why does it help?"). Before, Frederick: "Saying sorry is hard because it means admitting a mistake. It helps because it fixes things." Chloe: "A real sorry is small and quiet and means a lot." Now, Frederick: "Sorry is hard to say, because being wrong feels bad. But I have seen a sorry fix things." Chloe: "To me, a real sorry sounds soft and quiet, and it comes from your heart." Georgette: "My faith teaches me that sorry and forgiving go together, like two hands clapping." Mike: "I used to say sorry really fast to get it over with. Slow and real works better."
  - w-lost-game ("How does it feel to lose a game, and what can you do with that feeling?"). Before, Frederick: "Losing feels bad for a little while. Then you get another go." Chloe: "The people who lose the most games are the ones who play the most." Now, Frederick: "I have noticed that the people who lose the most games are the ones who play the most." Chloe: "Losing feels like a gray cloud to me. Then the cloud drifts away, and I feel light again." Georgette: "When I lost at checkers, I took a slow breath and asked for one more game." Mike: "Is losing really so bad? Every game I lost showed me a move to try next time."
  - w-cannot-yet ("What is the difference between I cannot do it and I cannot do it yet?"). Before, Frederick: "Yet is a small word that means you are still on the way." Chloe: "Every artist was once someone who could not draw yet." Now, Frederick: "Technically, it is one small word. But yet means you are still on the way." Chloe: "Every artist was once someone who could not draw yet. Even me!" Georgette: "I believe yet is one of the most hopeful words there is. It keeps the door open." Mike: "Before I say I cannot, I count my tries. Was it ten times, or just once?"
  - w-hard-is-good ("When something is hard, does that mean you are bad at it?"). Before, Frederick: "Hard means your brain is working. That is when it grows." Chloe: "If it was easy, you would already know it." Now, Frederick: "I read that when you keep practicing something hard, your brain builds new paths." Chloe: "If it were easy, you would already know it. I look for the hard part on purpose." Georgette: "Reading was hard for me at first. Now my reading room is full of books!" Mike: "Does hard mean bad? I am not so sure. Sometimes hard just means try a new way."
  - w-stuck ("What can you do when you feel stuck?"). Before, Frederick: "Stuck is a normal part of learning. A break, a question, or a new way usually unsticks it." Chloe: "Sometimes the best thing is to step back and look from further away." Now, Frederick: "In my lab, when I get stuck, a short break or a fresh idea usually gets me going." Chloe: "When I am stuck on a painting, I step back and look from far away. It helps!" Georgette: "I ask for help when I am stuck, and sometimes I say a quiet prayer too." Mike: "I check if I am stuck or just tired. If I am tired, I rest first."
  - w-good-and-bad-same-day ("Can a day be good and bad at the same time?"). Before, Frederick: "Most days are a mix. That is what days are like." Chloe: "A picture with only bright colors is not a real picture." Now, Frederick: "If you measure a day hour by hour, most days are a mix of good and hard." Chloe: "I think a painting with only bright colors looks flat. Shadows make the bright parts shine." Georgette: "On my hardest days, I still find one good thing, and I am thankful for it." Mike: "When I say a day was bad, I check. Was it all bad, or one bad thing?"
  - w-feelings-pass ("Do feelings last forever?"). Before, Frederick: "Feelings come like weather. Even big ones pass." Chloe: "A storm feels like it will never end, and then it does." Now, Frederick: "I have watched my own feelings like an experiment. Even my biggest ones got smaller with time." Chloe: "When I am sad, I paint it blue. Days later, I often paint the same thing yellow." Georgette: "Each time I pray, I remember that hard feelings come and go, like night and morning." Mike: "Some feelings, like loving my family, last a very long time. I hope those ones stay!"
  - w-everyone-different ("Is it okay to be different from everyone else?"). Before, Frederick: "No two people are the same. Different is how people come." Chloe: "The best pictures are the ones nobody else could have made." Now, Frederick: "I once looked at twins' fingerprints with a magnifying glass. Even twins have different ones!" Chloe: "The pictures I love most are the ones nobody else could have made. Just like you." Georgette: "I believe every person is made with care, and no two are the same." Mike: "I asked my friends if they ever feel different. Every one said yes, so I am not alone!"
  - w-ocean-deep ("How deep is the ocean?"). Before, Frederick: "The deepest part is so deep that a mountain would disappear in it." Chloe: "Nobody has seen most of the ocean. Imagine what is down there." Now, Frederick: "It turns out the tallest mountain could fit inside the deepest part of the ocean!" Chloe: "Most of the ocean has never been seen by people. I like imagining what lives down there." Georgette: "Looking out at the sea fills me with wonder. I like to say a little thank-you for it." Mike: "How would anyone measure something so deep? Sailors used to lower long ropes, and now ships use sound."
  - w-cat-purr ("Why do cats purr?"). Before, Frederick: "Cats purr when they are happy, and sometimes when they are hurt too. Nobody knows all of why." Chloe: "A purr sounds like a tiny, happy engine." Now, Frederick: "Scientists have found that cats purr when happy, and sometimes when hurt. Nobody knows all the reasons yet." Chloe: "To me, a purr sounds like a tiny, happy engine." Georgette: "As a girl, I had a cat who purred on my lap every time I read a book." Mike: "Maybe a purr is happy talk. I would watch when a cat purrs, and when it stays quiet."
  - w-old-people-know ("Why do older people know so many things?"). Before, Frederick: "They have had more days to learn things in. Every day adds a little." Chloe: "Ask an older person you know a question, and watch what happens." Now, Frederick: "I once counted my grandpa's days. He had lived over thirty thousand, and learned something every day!" Chloe: "Listening to older people is my favorite. Their stories are like treasure boxes waiting to open." Georgette: "Well, I have read a lot of books and lived a lot of days. Both helped me!" Mike: "Older people taught me a lot. I still check things myself, because the world keeps changing."
  - w-help-someone ("How does it feel to help someone?"). Before, Frederick: "Helping someone makes your own brain feel good. It is built that way." Chloe: "The smallest help can be the biggest thing in the day of someone else." Now, Frederick: "Scientists keep finding that helping others often gives the helper a happy feeling too." Chloe: "The smallest help, like holding a door, can light up someone's whole day." Georgette: "Helping someone always fills my heart. I believe that is how we were made." Mike: "I have noticed helping can feel great, and tiring too. So I help in small, steady ways."
  - w-big-or-small ("Are you big or small?"). Before, Frederick: "You are bigger than a mouse and smaller than a horse." Chloe: "Next to a mountain, everyone is small." Now, Frederick: "Technically, you are bigger than a mouse and smaller than a horse." Chloe: "I think, when you are next to a mountain, everyone feels small." Georgette: "I have always believed that small ones matter just as much as big ones." Mike: "Grown-ups call you big one day and too small the next. I ask, big enough for what?"
  - w-same-or-different ("Are you and a friend the same, or different?"). Before, Frederick: "Let's test it! Ask a friend their favorite food, and listen. Is it your favorite too?" Chloe: "When I paint two friends, I look for what matches, and then for what does not." Now, Frederick: "I like to collect clues. Ask a friend their favorite food, and see if it matches yours." Chloe: "When I paint two friends, I look for what matches first, then for what does not." Georgette: "Meeting someone very different from me is my favorite way to learn something new." Mike: "The same in what way? You might both love pizza and go to bed at different times."
  - w-where-sun-goes ("Where does the sun go at night?"). Before, Frederick: "The sun does not go anywhere. The Earth turns us away from it." Chloe: "Somewhere it is morning right now, and the sun is there." Now, Frederick: "Technically, the sun does not leave. The Earth turns our side away from it, and that is night." Chloe: "While you sleep, I picture children far away waking up to their morning. It makes me smile." Georgette: "Long ago, people told stories of the sun sailing a boat through the night. I love those stories." Mike: "Try this with a grown-up. Turn a ball slowly by a lamp, and watch day and night happen."
  - w-fish-home ("A fish needs water, and many birds need trees. What does your home give you?"). Before, Frederick: "Every living thing needs a place that gives it what it needs." Chloe: "A home is the place where you can be yourself." Now, Frederick: "I study animal homes. Every animal needs food, water and a safe spot, and so do people!" Chloe: "To me, home is where I can wear my comfiest socks and just be myself." Georgette: "I have always found that home is more than walls. It is people who care." Mike: "Does a home have to be a house? I have friends who live on boats!"
  - w-quiet-sound ("What is the quietest sound you can hear right now?"). Before, Frederick: "Close your eyes and listen. There is always a small sound somewhere." Chloe: "Quiet sounds are hiding under the loud ones." Now, Frederick: "Here is something amazing. Your ears keep working all the time, even when you are not listening." Chloe: "Quiet sounds are my favorite music, like a clock ticking or a cat breathing." Georgette: "When I want quiet, I sit by my round window with my tea and just listen." Mike: "I wonder if there is ever total silence. Maybe there is always some tiny sound."
  - w-ants-elephant ("Which is more, a big group of tiny ants or one elephant?"). Before, Frederick: "There are more ants, but the elephant is heavier." Chloe: "Ants make a wiggly line. An elephant is one big shape." Now, Frederick: "If you count, there are more ants. If you weigh them, one elephant is heavier." Chloe: "Ants make a wiggly, dotty line, and an elephant is one big gray shape." Georgette: "I believe every creature matters, the tiniest ant and the biggest elephant alike." Mike: "When someone asks which is more, I ask, more what? The answer can change."
  - w-early-tower-fell ("Your block tower fell down. What do you do next?"). Before, Frederick: "A wide bottom helps a tower stand." Chloe: "Every tower you build is a new one." Now, Frederick: "A wide bottom helps a tower stand tall. I test that with my own blocks!" Chloe: "I think every new tower is a brand new chance to make something different." Georgette: "When my towers fell as a girl, I felt sad too. A slow breath helped me build again." Mike: "Let's look at how the tower fell, leaning or wobbling. That tells us what to change."
  - w-early-feeling-sad ("When you feel sad, what helps you feel better?"). Before, Frederick: "Telling someone how you feel can make it feel smaller." Georgette: "You are never alone when you are sad." Now, Frederick: "It turns out a warm hug can help a body calm down." Chloe: "Drawing my favorite place helps me when I am sad. It feels like a little trip there." Georgette: "When I am sad, I say a little prayer and have a cup of tea with a friend." Mike: "I check how long my sad feelings stay. If one stays long, tell a grown-up you trust."
  - w-early-gift-or-earned ("Your aunt gives you five dollars for your birthday. Did you earn it?"). Before, Frederick: "Money you work for is income. This was a gift." Chloe: "Draw a birthday card with money inside it." Now, Frederick: "I like clear names for things. Money you work for is earned, and birthday money is a gift." Chloe: "A gift feels like a warm surprise to me. Earning money makes me proud, like finishing a painting." Georgette: "Whenever someone gives me a gift, I say thank you, and I try to give gifts too." Mike: "What if your aunt said the money was for helping in her garden? Then maybe you earned it!"
  - w-early-spent-it-all ("You spent all your money on a toy. Then you saw something you wanted more. What can you do?"). Before, Frederick: "Save a little each week, and it adds up." Chloe: "Draw the thing you want on your saving jar." Now, Frederick: "Here is some math I love. One coin every week adds up to a nice little pile." Chloe: "I would draw the thing I want and tape it to my saving jar. It keeps me excited!" Georgette: "Everyone has spent money and then wished they had waited. I have too, many times." Mike: "Before I spend, I ask one question. Do I want this more than anything else?"
  - w-early-both-right ("You think a picture looks happy. Your friend thinks it looks sad. Who is right?"). Before, Chloe: "A picture can be two things at once." Mike: "Ask each other what you saw." Now, Frederick: "From what I have seen, the same picture can make two people feel different things." Chloe: "I hope my paintings feel happy to some people and sad to others. Then they are really looking!" Georgette: "Two people at one window can see two different skies. I like to listen to both." Mike: "Point to the happy part and the sad part. Maybe you were looking at different corners!"
  - w-early-lost-the-beat ("You clapped along to a song and lost the beat in front of everyone. What now?"). Before, Frederick: "Tap your foot first. Then your hands can follow." Chloe: "Everyone loses the beat; music waits for you." Now, Frederick: "If you listen closely, the beat keeps going even when you stop. It is always there to catch." Chloe: "Losing the beat feels wobbly, like a missed step. Musicians do it sometimes, me too!" Georgette: "In my long life, I have learned that people remember your smile, not your missed clap." Mike: "Hmm, clapping louder just makes the miss louder. I would go quiet, listen, then come back in."
  - w-early-the-coat-monster ("A coat in the dark looked like a monster. Was your brain being silly?"). Before, Frederick: "Your brain guesses fast in the dark to keep you safe." Georgette: "Turn on the light and thank your brain." Now, Frederick: "I read that in the dark, brains guess fast to keep us safe. Mine would rather be careful!" Chloe: "I think your brain was drawing a story in the dark, the way I do on paper." Georgette: "Every child meets that coat, me too. A hug from someone you love makes the dark feel smaller." Mike: "Let's check with the light on. A monster that is a coat every time is a coat!"
  - w-early-i-forgot-my-line ("You forgot your line in the class play. What now?"). Before, Frederick: "Breathe, then say it again a little every day." Chloe: "Every actor forgets a line once." Now, Frederick: "It turns out a worried brain can drop words. It happens to grown-ups too, even me!" Chloe: "I forgot my line in a play once. I giggled, took a breath, and then I remembered." Georgette: "My students forgot lines in almost every play. One lost line is a small thing that feels big." Mike: "Giving up on plays over one line is like giving up lunch over one dropped fork!"
  - w-early-is-a-stick-a-toy ("Is a stick a toy?"). Before, Frederick: "Say what a toy is first." Chloe: "A stick can be anything you like." Now, Frederick: "I would test the stick. Give it to a friend and watch. Do they play with it?" Chloe: "A stick can be a magic wand, a horse, or a fishing pole, all in one afternoon!" Georgette: "When I was little, our best toy was a stick, and the second best was a box!" Mike: "What makes a toy a toy? A pot and a spoon can make a great drum!"
  - w-early-lost-my-turn ("You talked when it was not your turn and your friend got sad. What now?"). Before, Georgette: "Say sorry, then listen with your brain and your body." Mike: "Everyone slips; the next turn is a fresh one." Now, Frederick: "I count to three in my head before I talk. It gives my friend time to finish." Chloe: "I think your friend just wanted to be heard. Ask them to say it again." Georgette: "In my classroom, a real sorry, then listening with your brain and body, fixed most troubles." Mike: "Talking louder makes it worse, and you never need to stop talking forever. Next turn, try again!"
  - w-early-two-wants ("You have coins for one thing and you want two things. What do you do?"). Before, Frederick: "Choosing one means the other waits, not disappears." Chloe: "The one you still think about tomorrow is the one." Now, Frederick: "I count my coins first. If they buy one thing, the other one waits for my next coins." Chloe: "I like to wait until morning. The one I still want when I wake up is the one." Georgette: "Every grown-up makes this choice every week. I try to be glad about the one I picked." Mike: "Let's think about which one lasts longer. A toy that breaks by Friday is not much fun."
  - w-early-jar-broke ("You saved for weeks, then spent it all in one day and felt bad. What now?"). Before, Frederick: "The jar can start again tomorrow." Mike: "Make the rule before you walk into the store." Now, Frederick: "When my experiments fail, I start again, a little smarter. Your jar can start again tomorrow too!" Chloe: "To me, that icky feeling is a little teacher. It will remind you next time." Georgette: "Money mistakes happen to me too. Being kind to myself always comes first." Mike: "I make my spending rule at home. In the store, shiny toys make it too hard to think!"
  - w-early-robot-bumped ("Your robot walked into a rock. What do you do next?"). Before, Frederick: "A bump shows you which step to change." Mike: "Watch it again before you change anything." Now, Frederick: "My little robot does exactly what its steps say. So a bump shows me which step to fix." Chloe: "I would draw the path on paper first. A picture of the walk is easy to check." Georgette: "A bump is not a failure, dear. It is the robot telling you something new." Mike: "Before I change anything, I watch the robot walk again. Then I know just where it bumped."
  - w-early-where-milk-starts ("Your milk came from the store. Where was it before the store?"). Before, Frederick: "Milk comes from cows on a dairy farm." Chloe: "Picture a cow, a truck and a store in a row." Now, Frederick: "I visited a dairy farm once. Cows get milked every day, and cold trucks carry the milk away." Chloe: "I picture it like a little parade, a cow, a shiny truck, a store, and your cup." Georgette: "A farmer got up early to care for the cows. I say a little thank-you for farmers." Mike: "Next time, look at the carton with a grown-up. Some cartons name the farm or the dairy!"
  - w-early-my-plant-drooped ("You forgot to water your plant, and now it is drooping. What can you do?"). Before, Frederick: "A droopy plant is thirsty. Give it water and wait." Georgette: "Everybody forgets sometimes. Try again today." Now, Frederick: "I study plants. A droopy one is often thirsty, and water can help it stand back up." Chloe: "I love watching the leaves lift slowly after a drink, like someone waking up from a nap." Georgette: "Every gardener forgets to water sometimes, even me. Plants forgive more than we think." Mike: "Let's check the soil first with one finger. Dry means water it, and wet means wait."
  - w-early-hand-up-forever ("You put your hand up and waited, and three other friends got turns first. Was that fair?"). Before, Frederick: "Every turn is one talker. Yours is coming." Chloe: "Waiting is part of the game, like the quiet between songs." Now, Frederick: "When everyone talks at once, I notice nobody is heard well. So turns line up. Yours is coming!" Chloe: "I think waiting with your hand up feels long, like the quiet between two songs." Georgette: "Waiting is hard at five and hard at eighty. I still wiggle when I wait!" Mike: "Count the hands next time. If yours was up first, tell the teacher kindly."
  - w-early-forgot-the-last-step ("The teacher said three steps, and you did two and forgot the last one. What now?"). Before, Frederick: "Ask for the last step. Asking is how you get it right." Georgette: "Two out of three is nearly there. Ask, and finish." Now, Frederick: "I act out each step as I hear it. That helps all three steps stick in my head!" Chloe: "I picture the steps like three stones in a row. The third stone is still waiting for you." Georgette: "I always smiled when a student asked about a forgotten step. Two out of three is nearly there!" Mike: "Hmm, guessing might give you the wrong step. Asking gets you the right one."
  - w-early-computer-told ("A computer only does what it is told. Is that good, or not so good?"). Before, Frederick: "It does every step you give it, and no more." Chloe: "You are the one with the ideas." Now, Frederick: "Technically, a computer does every step you give it, and not one more." Chloe: "I think you are the artist with the ideas, and the computer is your paintbrush." Georgette: "People can stop, think, and choose to be kind. A computer needs us to tell it carefully." Mike: "Wrong steps make a computer do the wrong thing just as fast. So I always check the steps."
  - w-early-spilled-on-my-picture ("You spilled water on your picture. Is it ruined?"). Before, Chloe: "A spill can turn into a cloud or a puddle." Frederick: "Watch how the water spreads. It makes new shapes." Now, Frederick: "With paint or markers, water carries some color along the paper. That makes soft new edges!" Chloe: "Spills can make lovely shapes. I once turned a spill into a rain cloud in my picture!" Georgette: "A spill would make me sad too. But you made your picture once, so you can make another!" Mike: "Wait until the paper dries before you decide. Wet paper looks darker than it will later."
  - w-early-stuck-zipper ("You tried and tried to zip your coat, and it kept getting stuck. What now?"). Before, Frederick: "Your hands learn a little more every time you try." Mike: "Pull gently. Pulling harder can make it stick more." Now, Frederick: "I checked once, and pulling harder only jammed my zipper more. Slow and gentle works better." Chloe: "My hands get wobbly when I rush. So I rest them a moment, then try the zipper again." Georgette: "Asking for help is not giving up. I still ask, and someday you will teach someone to zip!" Mike: "I look closely at the exact spot where the zipper catches. Then I fix just that spot."
  - w-early-outside-the-lines ("You colored outside the lines. Is that a mistake?"). Before, Chloe: "Lines are a helper, not a rule." Frederick: "Hands get steadier the more you color." Now, Frederick: "Scientists have found that hands keep getting steadier for years. Coloring inside small lines takes time!" Chloe: "Lots of artists paint past the lines on purpose. To me, lines are a helper, not a rule." Georgette: "Nobody has to be perfect to make something lovely. I keep every picture my students give me." Mike: "A mistake is when you meant one thing and did another. On purpose is a choice!"
  - w-early-missed-the-ball ("You kicked at the ball and missed it. What do you do next?"). Before, Frederick: "Your eyes tell your foot where to go." Chloe: "Every good player has missed the ball lots of times." Now, Frederick: "I tested my own kicks once. Every miss helped my eyes, brain and legs practice teamwork!" Chloe: "Even great players miss the ball. To me, a miss is just one moment, not the whole game." Georgette: "I have watched many children learn to kick, and every one missed at first. Then they tried again!" Mike: "If you are tired, rest. But if you just feel silly, stay and kick again!"
  - w-early-shoes-wrong-feet ("Your shoes are on the wrong feet. Is that a big mistake?"). Before, Frederick: "Your feet can tell. The shoes feel squished and funny." Georgette: "Everybody does this sometimes. Switch them and off you go." Now, Frederick: "Most shoes curve to fit one foot, I checked! So the wrong one feels squished." Chloe: "I put half a sticker in each shoe. When the halves make one picture, my shoes are right!" Georgette: "Every grown-up you know has done this, and some of us still do it when we rush!" Mike: "I ask how long a mistake takes to fix. Ten seconds means it is a tiny one!"
  - w-early-missing-someone ("When you miss someone you love, what can you do?"). Before, Frederick: "Missing someone shows how much they matter to you." Chloe: "A picture can carry your love to someone far away." Now, Frederick: "I have noticed that missing someone comes from caring about them. Grown-ups feel it too." Chloe: "When I miss someone, I draw us doing something we love together. It feels like a visit." Georgette: "I hold the people I miss in my heart, and sometimes I say a little prayer for them." Mike: "Missing someone hurts, and that is okay. Telling a grown-up you trust can make it lighter."
  - w-early-not-asked-to-play ("Your friends are playing a game and did not ask you. How do you feel?"). Before, Frederick: "Being left out hurts. That hurt is real, and lots of people feel it." Mike: "Try asking to join. Maybe they just forgot to ask." Now, Frederick: "Scientists have found that being left out hurts almost everyone, even grown-ups." Chloe: "Being left out feels like a small, heavy cloud in my chest. That feeling is real and okay." Georgette: "I was left out sometimes as a girl. Now I always look for anyone standing alone." Mike: "Before deciding they left you out on purpose, check. Maybe they did not see you!"
  - w-early-slow-breaths ("When a feeling gets very big, can slow breaths help it get smaller?"). Before, Frederick: "Long, slow breaths out help your body calm down." Chloe: "Pretend to smell a flower, then pretend to blow out a candle, slowly." Now, Frederick: "Here is something true. Long, slow breaths out can help your body calm down." Chloe: "Pretend to smell a flower, then pretend to blow out a candle, slowly. I do it too." Georgette: "When my heart feels heavy, I sit quietly and breathe slowly. Sometimes I pray too." Mike: "Do not just take my word for it. Try five slow breaths, and notice how you feel."
  - w-early-feeling-shy ("Is it okay to feel shy when you meet someone new?"). Before, Frederick: "Lots of people feel shy at first. It often fades as you get to know someone." Chloe: "Quiet watching is a fine way to start." Now, Frederick: "It turns out feeling shy is very common. It often fades as you get to know someone new." Chloe: "I think shy people are often great watchers, and watching is a big part of art." Georgette: "Even now I feel shy sometimes. A small smile and a soft hello are enough." Mike: "Shy is a feeling, not a rule about you. I bet the new person feels shy too!"
  - w-early-grown-up-said-no ("A grown-up said no to something you really wanted. What helps the mad feeling?"). Before, Frederick: "A mad feeling is biggest at the start. It usually shrinks with time." Mike: "Ask why, in a calm voice. There may be a good reason." Now, Frederick: "I timed my own mad feelings once. They were biggest at the start, then shrank minute by minute." Chloe: "When I feel mad, I draw something I love, like a garden. My busy hands calm me down." Georgette: "I often said no to keep my students safe. You can say how you feel, calmly and kindly." Mike: "Ask why, in a calm voice. Not now is not the same as never!"
  - w-early-pretend-hero ("A job feels long and boring, and you want to stop. What could help you keep going?"). Before, Frederick: "Kids who pretended to be a hard-working hero kept going longer." Chloe: "Picture a hero who keeps going. Do the job the way they would." Now, Frederick: "Scientists found that kids who pretended to be a hard-working hero kept going longer." Chloe: "On a long painting, I take a short break and look out my window. Then I keep going!" Georgette: "When a job gets long, I think of my grandmother. She never rushed and never quit." Mike: "Does pretending really help? Test it. Do a job as you, then again as your hero."
  - w-early-tired-and-cranky ("When you are very tired, do little problems feel bigger?"). Before, Frederick: "A tired body makes feelings bigger. Sleep helps shrink them back." Chloe: "Tired eyes see a gray world. Rested eyes see more color." Now, Frederick: "I read about toddlers who skipped one nap. They got upset more easily and smiled less." Chloe: "When I am tired, my colors come out muddy. After a rest, I see everything fresh." Georgette: "My grandmother always said, everything looks better after a good night's sleep." Mike: "Next time something feels terrible, I ask myself, am I just tired? Often, yes!"
  - w-early-drawing-in-my-head ("Your drawing came out different from the picture in your head. Is it a bad drawing?"). Before, Chloe: "Every artist feels this. The picture in your head is something to aim for." Frederick: "Your hands get better at drawing every time you try." Now, Frederick: "Even my microscope drawings never match perfectly. Drawing what you picture is a skill that grows for years!" Chloe: "Every artist feels this, me too. The picture in my head is something to aim for." Georgette: "A drawing made with care is a good drawing to me, whatever it looks like." Mike: "Bad compared to what? Compare it to last month's drawing, not the one in your head."
  - w-early-said-it-wrong ("You said a word wrong, and someone giggled. What do you do?"). Before, Frederick: "Some sounds are hard to say. Lots of kids learn them later." Mike: "Maybe they giggled because it sounded funny, not to be mean." Now, Frederick: "I read that the sound at the start of thumb is one of the last sounds children learn." Chloe: "I practice tricky words slowly, clapping each part like a drumbeat." Georgette: "My faith teaches me to be gentle when someone makes a mistake, and gentle with myself too." Mike: "Was the giggle mean, or was the word just funny? People often laugh at sounds, not at you."
  - w-early-paper-plane-crashed ("Your paper airplane crashed right away. What do you do next?"). Before, Frederick: "Each crash is a test. It shows you what to change next." Mike: "Change just one thing at a time. Then you know what helped." Now, Frederick: "My heroes, the Wright brothers, tested lots of wing shapes before their first airplane flew." Chloe: "I make sharp folds and matching wings, like a mirror. And I always give my plane a name!" Georgette: "Long ago, some people said nobody would ever fly. I am so glad someone kept trying!" Mike: "Change just one thing at a time. Then you will know what helped."
  - w-early-broke-a-friends-toy ("You broke your friend's toy by accident. What do you do?"). Before, Georgette: "A real sorry, and an offer to help, can mend a lot." Frederick: "Your friend may still feel sad, even though it was an accident." Now, Frederick: "I once broke a friend's toy by accident. He felt sad, though I did not mean it." Chloe: "In Japan, some broken bowls are fixed with gold along the cracks. I think that is beautiful." Georgette: "My grandmother taught me that a real sorry tells what happened and offers to help." Mike: "Is hiding a broken toy easier? I tried it once, and it made everything worse."
  - w-early-helping-made-a-mess ("You tried to help wash the dishes, and water went everywhere. Was helping a mistake?"). Before, Frederick: "Even toddlers want to help. Helping well just takes practice." Mike: "Helping was good. Too much water was the part to change." Now, Frederick: "Scientists found that even toddlers help without being asked. Wanting to help starts very young!" Chloe: "Every new job is a little messy at first, like my first paintings. I love a messy start!" Georgette: "In my kitchen, a helper with wet sleeves is still a helper. We clean up together." Mike: "I would say helping was good, and too much water was the part to change."
  - w-early-bad-dream ("You woke up from a scary dream. What helps you feel safe again?"). Before, Frederick: "Bad dreams are common in young children. A dream cannot hurt you." Chloe: "Draw your dream again, and give it a happy ending." Now, Frederick: "From what scientists know, bad dreams are common in children, and a dream cannot hurt you." Chloe: "In the morning, I draw my bad dream with a new, happy ending. I get to choose!" Georgette: "When I was little, my mother sat with me after bad dreams until I felt calm." Mike: "Dreams can feel real, so I check. My own bed and blanket tell me I am safe."
  - w-early-thunder-booms ("A thunderstorm is booming outside. What helps when you feel scared?"). Before, Frederick: "Count after the flash. Five seconds means the lightning is about a mile away." Mike: "When you hear thunder, go inside. Inside is the safest place." Now, Frederick: "I count after every flash. The longer I count before the boom, the farther away the lightning is." Chloe: "To me, thunder sounds like giant drums rolling across the sky." Georgette: "When storms came at night, my family sat close, and we sang and prayed until they passed." Mike: "Being scared of thunder makes sense. When you can hear thunder, stay inside, away from windows."
  - w-early-shot-at-the-doctor ("You need a shot at the doctor. What helps you feel brave?"). Before, Frederick: "Looking at something else, or slow breaths, can make a shot hurt less." Georgette: "Holding a hand you love makes hard things easier." Now, Frederick: "Looking at something else, or breathing slowly, can make a shot hurt less. Scientists tested it!" Chloe: "I count the colors on a picture on the wall. The shot is over before I know it." Georgette: "I held my mother's hand tight at the doctor when I was small. Holding on is brave too." Mike: "Let's test which trick works best for you. Try one this time, and another next time."
  - w-early-someone-grabbed-my-toy ("Someone grabbed your toy without asking. What do you do?"). Before, Frederick: "Anger makes your body hot and fast. A slow breath helps you think." Mike: "Say it calmly: I was playing with that. Please give it back." Now, Frederick: "My heart beats fast when someone grabs my things. One slow breath lets my thinking catch up." Chloe: "A calm, strong voice can sound braver than yelling. I practiced mine with a stuffed bunny." Georgette: "I believe in treating others the way I want to be treated, even when they forget." Mike: "Grabbing it back might work for a second, but then two people are mad instead of one."
  - w-early-trip-canceled ("A fun trip got canceled because of the rain. What helps the sad feeling?"). Before, Frederick: "Feeling let down shows how much you were looking forward to it." Chloe: "Rainy days are good for building forts and drawing pictures." Now, Frederick: "I have noticed that the bigger the hope, the bigger the sad feeling. It shrinks with time." Chloe: "I feel sad too when plans change. Then I find one cozy thing to look forward to." Georgette: "I believe every day holds a gift, even a rainy one. We just have to find it." Mike: "Let's ask a grown-up for a new day. A trip moved to another day is still coming!"
  - w-early-bad-start ("Your morning went wrong: spilled cereal and a lost shoe. Will the whole day be bad?"). Before, Chloe: "A boy named Alexander had a very bad day in a famous book. Some days are like that." Mike: "Two bad things this morning do not mean the whole day is bad." Now, Frederick: "I look for what made each thing happen. The spilled cereal did not make your shoe go missing!" Chloe: "I love a famous book about Alexander's terrible, horrible day. Some days are just like that!" Georgette: "I start fresh at lunch with a deep breath. The morning does not decide the whole day." Mike: "Let's test the day. Count the good things that happen from now until bedtime, then decide!"
  - w-early-so-hard-to-wait ("Waiting for something you really want feels so long. What helps you wait?"). Before, Frederick: "Kids waited longer when they looked away and thought about something else." Mike: "Waiting is easier when you trust the promise will be kept." Now, Frederick: "Scientists found that kids waited longer when they looked away or sang a little song." Chloe: "I make a paper chain and tear off one loop each night. The wait gets shorter and shorter!" Georgette: "Before holidays, my family counts the days with songs. Waiting can be part of the joy." Mike: "I wait better when I know the grown-up will keep their promise. So I ask them first!"

### His notes
- "Blue, blue": speak() asked the voice again 700 ms after a request when the voice was quiet, for words the browser had dropped; a word as short as Blue is said and done inside 700 ms, so the quiet after it looked like a voice that never started and the word was said again. The retry now runs only when no part of the request began (onstart or onend). The test page's voice never reported speaking, so no test had seen it; question-screens now taps a word with a voice that does, and hears it once.

Now a pop-up on the overview names the lesson ("Tracing Letters needs a touch screen." and the line about an iPad), from the overview, the result's arrow or a story's arrow alike; Got it, the backdrop or Escape closes it, and Got it takes the focus.

- The place after a book: the app kept the overview's place as window.scrollY, which is always 0 in the claude.ai preview on a laptop, a frame as tall as the page whose page around it does the scrolling, so every book came back at the top there (in a normal window it already returned). readPlace and goToPlace keep the place in every kind of page: a normal window's scroll, a box's scroll, or in a page-tall frame the part of the page that showed (visibleBand, plus the frame's own scroll, since a page taller than its frame scrolls that too), given back by scrolling a marker at that spot to the top of the screen; the probes that measure it start when a page-tall frame's screen changes, so the first book after a refresh comes back too (the code and screen checks). A celebration's story ends at home, not at an old place; the Back arrows on a story opened from the shelf return to the place.

The other quiet lines inside games wait for EARMARKS L4.
- The space shooter: chips keep coming until the last of three ships is gone, each a little faster and a little sooner than the one before (0.006 board units a frame faster a chip to about 0.6 at chip 73, then 0.002 a chip with no ceiling; from 70 frames apart down to 30), a wave every five fitting chips hit, and the best is how many were hit ("12 hits" on its tile). A ship goes when a fitting chip gets past ("8 is one of the even numbers, and it got past.") or a shot hits one that does not fit. A chip never starts in line with a chip of the other kind: the two sit wholly side by side with a gap ("It can be slightly to the side though"), and a chip that does not fit never starts in a shot's lane, the ship's or where it is gliding, so a second quick tap never meets a wrong chip that came after it. The rules live in logic.mjs (shipStep, shipAdvance, shipLaneClear and the rest) and the rules test plays them: a careful player passes a hundred fitting chips in every game and still meets a speed it cannot keep up with; a child's taps anywhere across a chip, tapped twice, on a slow device three frames a step, never lose a ship to a wrong chip in the first 150; an idle player loses all three ships to chips that get past. A game closed or ended by the play clock counts how far it got. The words say ships and waves ("You have three ships, shown at the top ... Every five hits starts a new wave, and your score is how many you hit."), and the end card says "You got to wave W before your last ship was gone." A miss now costs a ship, which the game brief's item 5 forbids; that is Mikey's own exception ("go until failure"), written into item 5.
- The best score: the game check found that a best was lost five seconds after it was set (older than this pass): the play clock's save and its time-up wrote back the state of the moment the game opened. Both, and the score, now read the latest saved state (colorStateNow), and the time-up keeps the best.
- The Wonder review's words are his, word for word: "Early Learners", "Children who cannot read yet hear the wonder questions instead. They select an answer, also spoken, then hear four differing perspectives which will hopefully broaden their own.", and "For the readers:". The longer reader voices are tweaked by the early rules when their questions are reviewed, as he said.
- More Info read aloud: its speaker reads each description (a reason, why the answer fits, a more right example) with the sentence being read lit in the light green, a pause between descriptions (0.7 seconds, 1 second for an early learner) and, for an early learner, a voice 0.85 of its usual pace (speakSequence's new gap and rate; RichText's litLine lights the line of an explanation written one sentence a line). It keeps its utterances held, as speak() does, and stops itself when the voice goes quiet without ending (the code check).

That is why I wear my red coat everywhere!" became "I am thankful for every color, and red makes me happiest. Every person sees them a little differently, so the color that makes you happiest might look a little different to someone else." became "Technically, the colors you see start as light. Light bounces off a strawberry and into your eyes. Tiny cells at the back of your eyes, called cones, catch that light, and your brain turns their signals into the red you see. Scientists who study favorite colors have found that people tend to like the colors of things they like, such as a clear blue sky. So when a color makes me happy, I ask what it reminds me of."; Chloe: "Painters spend their whole lives choosing colors. There is no wrong favorite. Try painting something in your color, and notice how the picture makes you feel."; Georgette: "Many people see the colors of the world as a gift to be enjoyed. Whatever you believe, it is a fine thing to stop and notice a color you love." became "I believe the colors of the world are a gift, and I try to say thank you for them, like the green of new grass after a spring rain. Red has made me happiest for as long as I can remember, which is why my red coat goes nearly everywhere with me. Whatever you believe, it is a fine thing to stop and notice a color you love."; Mike: "Would you pick the same color tomorrow? It might change, and that is interesting. Try asking yourself again next week and see." became "My favorite color keeps changing, so I hold my answer loosely. When I was little, red was my favorite, and these days it is blue, at least this week. Here is a test you can try. Pick your color again tomorrow and next week, and keep track. If your answer changes, you have not failed the test. You found out something new about yourself, and that is what a test is for."

### The workflow, read against the paper and the trust pyramid
- Three read-only checks measured it first, on pass ML's copy. (1) The kinds of mistake the checks found in passes MA to ML: 35 classes read from DECISIONS, ranked by the passes they came back in times their harm, each with the strongest check that held it and a proposed one, with 255 quotes of evidence, each checked by script (docs/MISTAKE-CLASSES.md keeps them all). An unsafe scene for a young child came back in ten of the twelve passes, a wrong or overgeneralized fact in nine, a moral out of step with its spoken lesson in eight, a standard not quoted whole and word for word in seven, and the record misstating its source, and a fix that broke something else, in all twelve. A check that reads a whole population for a structural property had ended its class every time (Overlay, layout as variety, ages, careers, no "actually"); one that matched a wording moved the mistake to the next wording. (2) What a new chat loads: about 754 KB of start-of-chat reading, CLAUDE.md alone 186 KB of 382 dated lines, loaded into every session and every checking agent (about 838,000 tokens across pass ML's eighteen agents), some of its lines replaced by later lines that never said so (sentence length, story length, the setup line, the paper's color, the unlock rule, the home button, the tags). (3) How strongly the pre-K content was verified: every main-loop check passed on 20,000 seeds of all 144 pre-K banks, but seeds 1 to 300 never made 880 of the 3,037 distinct pre-K questions and 33 banks had no derivation of their answer, so a wrong answer key would have been caught in 59.4 percent of pre-K questions (26.9 percent in this course); a wrong answer planted in a question first made at seed 890 passed the whole rules test, and the content comparison saw no change.
- What changed, best first by the pyramid, each check proven failing on a real past mistake and its near misses before it was kept:
  - The standards' own texts are in the project (docs/standards/: the 2022 Texas Prekindergarten Guidelines for PK3 and PK4 whole, and the Head Start ELOF preschool goals with their 36 to 48 and 48 to 60 month progressions, transcribed by five readers, and the two indicators pre-K 3 quotes), and the coverage test holds every quote of every pre-K citation to them and to its plan row; it found six misquotes in pre-K 3 (", for example" for "(e.g., ...)" four times, ", receptive," for "(receptive)" twice) that the word-for-word readings of passes MJ and MK had passed, all fixed.
  - The rules test's per-question checks run as one function of the question, so every question a pre-K bank can make is read (seeds doubling while the last half still makes a new one, to 76,800) and read again with its answer key swapped for each wrong choice, which a check other than More Info's must catch; the 31 banks with no derivation gained one (PREK_DERIVE: from the words asked, the picture shown or the things drawn, and the helpers, tools and good choices from First Steps' own lessons). A wrong key planted in a question first made at seed 2005 was caught when the check was built.
  - Two whole-population checks in the stories test: a pre-reader's moral echoes its spoken lines (a sentence of the script word for word, or four in five of its content words; seven reviewed paraphrases kept by name, 44 morals of unreviewed courses waiting by name), and no pre-K story, lesson or picture holds a choking hazard without its reason (the experiments' list, widened; thirteen reasons).
  - No choice bank keeps its answer in one place (eight did, all shuffled after their own draws, so no seed's question changed), a bank whose answer never changes is listed (A31), and since round two a bank whose answer leans to one place waits by name too.
  - tools/content-snapshot.mjs keys every exported item, every distinct question with all its renderings, every ledger row and review mark, and tools/content-diff.mjs compares two copies item by item, outside the pass's scope first; the final read starts from it.
  - CLAUDE.md is the short manual (lines 1 to 113, a section on how it works, 56 dated lines a coder needs most, word for word, and a list of where kept lines have gone stale), under 40,000 bytes by test; the whole file as it stood through pass ML is docs/CLAUDE-HISTORY.md, and NEW-CHAT's pass history docs/NEW-CHAT-HISTORY.md, each held unchanged by a hash. Nothing was deleted.
  - RULES-AUDIT section 9 records the pyramid as the rule for where a new rule goes, and INDEPENDENT-CHECKS says in each brief what the machines now hold, so a reader reads what only a reader can.
  - docs/PROJECT-CONTEXT.md is the Project Context document Mikey asked for: the slow-changing picture (the vision, the roles, the two rules above all others, how the teaching works as one system, standards, pictures and audio, his standing preferences, how a chat works, how we keep it right, where things live, the plan), which says the zip wins wherever they differ.
- What did not change: the flow Mikey named, rounds of fresh agents on frozen copies, every finding read against its source before it is applied, second reads of every fix, his answers by number. The two-hour part of the vision is not leaned on; the checks serve depth and accuracy.
- Not built now, and why: the other classes' proposed checks wait in docs/MISTAKE-CLASSES.md, to be built when each class next comes up, highest rank first (EARMARKS L16), since each needs its own design and proof; the full game layout audit stays out of check.sh (553 seconds over 160 games at five sizes), and the two spills it found in other courses are earmarked (A33).

### Every Wonder line this pass changed (quoted for Mikey's later check, his rule since pass MB)
1 of the 366 Wonder questions changed.
- w-quiet-sound ("What is the quietest sound you can hear right now?"): its choices My breath, The wind and Not sure became My breath, A sound far away and Not sure; its closing "Close your eyes and count the sounds you can hear. How many did you find?" became "Close your eyes and listen. How many sounds can you count?"; the short voices: Georgette: "When I want quiet, I sit by my round window with my tea and just listen." became "When I want quiet, I sit by my round window with my tea. I listen, and I feel thankful."; Mike: "I wonder if there is ever total silence. Maybe there is always some tiny sound." became "I wonder if a room is ever all the way quiet. Every time I check, I hear one more tiny sound."; the reader voices: Frederick: "Your ears are always working, even when you are not listening. Close your eyes for a moment and the small sounds come forward: a clock, a bird, your own breath. They were there all along, waiting under the louder ones." became "Technically, your ears never switch off, not even while you sleep. Your brain does something clever, though. It gets used to steady sounds, like the hum of a fridge, and stops pointing them out to you. A loud sound can cover up a soft one too. Here is an experiment I like. Cup your hands behind your ears and listen again. The sounds in front of you get a little louder, because your hands catch more of them."; Chloe: "Musicians practice listening for the quietest sounds, because that is where a song gets its feeling. Try sitting still for the time it takes to count to ten and see how many sounds you can find." became "To me, quiet sounds are a kind of music. In 1952 a composer named John Cage wrote a piece with no notes in it. The first time it was played, a piano player sat at the piano for four minutes and thirty-three seconds and played nothing at all. The music was whatever the room gave, the wind outside, rain on the roof, people talking. When I paint outside, I listen that way first, and soft sounds make me reach for soft colors."; Georgette: "Many traditions make room for quiet on purpose, a moment before a meal or at the end of the day. Quiet is not an empty thing. It is where people notice what they were too busy to hear." became "I believe quiet is a gift, so I make room for it on purpose. When I was a girl, my grandmother kept a quiet moment before supper to say thank you. I still keep that moment, at my round window with a cup of tea. In that hush I can hear the clock and the birds, and my busy thoughts slow down. You do not have to believe what I believe to try a quiet minute and notice the small good things around you."; Mike: "Is there such a thing as total silence? People who sit in a room built to be perfectly quiet say they can hear their own heartbeat. So maybe there is no silence, only sounds we have stopped noticing." became "I used to think my room went totally silent at night, until I tested it. I lay very still and listened, and there was always something, a car far away, the house creaking, my own breathing. People have even built rooms that soak up almost every sound, and visitors who sit in them say they start to hear their own heartbeat. So now I never say a room is silent. I say it is very quiet, and I keep listening, in case I am wrong."

### Pre-K 4's last Domain I lesson
